title: 第七章　斯大林的墨水瓶：亚历山大·阿菲诺格诺夫

children: 在亚历山大·阿菲诺格诺夫广受欢迎的剧作《恐惧》（1931年首演）的一个关键场景中，资产阶级反射学教授博布罗夫与年轻的共产主义科学家叶莲娜就谁拥有改造人类和规划历史进程的合法权力——是资产阶级科学家还是共产主义政治家——展开了冲突。博布罗夫认为，只有科学家才能以“世纪的视角”思考；他们拥有文化权威，而且与政治家不同，他们不受日常紧迫问题的困扰：

In a key scene of Alexander Afinogenov’s popular play Fear, which pre-miered in 1931, Bobrov, a bourgeois professor of reflexology, clashes with the young Communist scientist Elena over who can claim legitimate authority to transform mankind and chart the course of history—bourgeois scientists or Communist politicians. Only scientists think in “the perspective of centuries,” Bobrov argues; they possess cultural authority and, unlike politicians, are not encumbered by pressing questions of the day:
博布罗夫：即使是最好的政治也迫使人们把时间像金钱一样浪费在琐事上……你知道国营农场“巨人”是第一个完成播种的……但你却忘记了《浮士德》的作者是谁。

Bobrov: Even the very best of politics compels one to waste time, like money, on details . . . You know that the State farm “The Giant” was the first to finish sowing . . . But you have forgotten who was the author of “Faust.”
叶莲娜：我没看过那部歌剧。
Elena: I haven’t seen that opera.
博布罗夫：容我提醒你，《浮士德》是拿来读的，不是拿来听的。你分不清一件塞夫勒瓷器和一只萨克森杯子的区别。
Bobrov: May I inform you that “Faust” should be read, not heard? You cannot tell the difference between a piece of Sèvres china and a Saxon cup.
叶莲娜：我用玻璃杯喝茶。
Elena: I drink tea out of a glass.
博布罗夫：历史把我们从一群猴子提升为精挑细选的文明人，而你们却在集体政治的研钵里碾碎这些棱角。
Bobrov: History has raised us from a herd of monkeys to select cultivated individuals, while you are crushing these facets in the mortar of collective politics.
叶莲娜：我们正在创造历史。你试着投入一次真实生活，你就会明白我们不只是在碾碎人的棱角。
Elena: We are making history. Try for once to involve yourself in real life, and you will understand that we are not just crushing facets.
《恐惧》使阿菲诺格诺夫——当时一位前途无量的年轻剧作家——成为苏联主要剧作家。该剧在莫斯科和列宁格勒首演，场场爆满。在十八个月的时间里，仅列宁格勒话剧院就演出了三百场；到20世纪30年代中期，该剧已成为整个苏联剧院节目的主要剧目。

《恐惧》展现了非苏联知识分子走向接受并拥护苏联政权的艰难道路。教授们开始明白，过去资产阶级的偏见扭曲了他们的研究，使他们相信所有人类行为都由基本的生理刺激决定，而在苏联背景下，最主要的刺激是恐惧：害怕政治偏差和清洗，害怕被捕和流放。他们声称，这种恐惧使苏联公民瘫痪，就像他们实验室里的兔子被巨蟒吓得瘫痪，并顺从地等待被其致命的拥抱碾碎一样。在剧中，教授们被像叶莲娜这样未经专业训练的年轻共产党员的热情活力所震惊，他们对社会主义充满了奉献精神。最终，他们意识到苏联政权作为这些杰出人物的创造者，提供了真正的“世纪视角”，他们热切地加入了集体建设运动。当叶莲娜（同时被任命为研究所所长）告诉博布罗夫她在一次短暂的出差中读了歌德的《浮士德》时，资产阶级科学与共产主义政治的幸福结合被敲定。这位急躁、学习迅速的年轻无产者在吸收资产阶级过去进步元素的同时，抛弃了一切被认为没有社会用途的东西。叶莲娜指挥了一场象征意义深远的集体公寓大扫除，指示博布罗夫清除一位拒绝放弃其过时生活方式的贵族女士的物品。

Fear established Afinogenov, up to then a promising young playwright, as a leading Soviet dramatist. The play premiered in Moscow and Leningrad and proved an instant sellout. Over the course of eighteen  months, the Leningrad Drama Theater alone presented three hundred performances; by the mid-1930s the play was a staple of theater programs throughout the Soviet realm.

Fear shows the difficult road traveled by the non-Soviet intelligentsia toward acceptance and embrace of the Soviet regime. The professors come to understand that in the past bourgeois prejudice distorted their research, leading them to believe that all human behavior was determined by basic physiological stimuli and that the overriding stimulus in the Soviet context was fear: of political deviations and purges, of arrest and deportation. This fear, they claimed, paralyzed Soviet citizens, much as the rabbits in their laboratory were paralyzed by the sight of a boa constrictor and submissively waited to be crushed in its deadly embrace. In the course of the play the professors are stunned by the enthusiastic energy of untrained young Communists like Elena, who burn with devotion to socialism. In the end they realize that the Soviet regime, as the creator of these exceptional people, furnishes the true “perspective of centuries,” and they eagerly join the collective construction campaign. The happy synthesis of bourgeois science and Communist politics is sealed when Elena, meanwhile appointed institute director, tells Bobrov that she has read Goethe’s Faust during a brief business trip. While this impatient, fast-learning young proletarian assimilates progressive elements of the bourgeois past, she discards everything deemed not of social use. Elena directs a symbolically fraught cleaning of her communal apartment, instructing Bobrov to remove the belongings of an aristocratic lady who refuses to abjure her outdated way of life.

剧中暗示，共产主义国家不像博布罗夫所担心的那样，会压垮所有个人。它邀请每一个真诚希望参与建设工作的人加入其集体。此外，它还培养了一代无畏、乐观的人民，他们将居住在社会主义的家园。只有那些将自己置于历史对立面、阻碍建设的人才会感到恐惧：他们连同其无用的物品一起，在“大扫除”中被扫除和碾碎，就像无用的塞夫勒瓷杯一样。

阿菲诺格诺夫在创作这部剧时，并未预见到1937年他自己会成为《恐惧》中所描述的清洗目标。随着斯大林主义大清洗的展开，吞噬了这位剧作家以及成千上万的其他人，他记录自己的经历不是以戏剧的形式，而是以个人日记的形式——可以说，这是一个私密的剧场，他在其中上演了自己人生的戏剧。阿菲诺格诺夫在20世纪30年代的生活也通过他的剧作、公开露面和私人信件得到了丰富的记录，他将威胁到他的清洗视为一个历史机遇时期。这是一个历史直接作用于他，他的生活戏剧被提升到世界历史层面的时刻。他将1937年视为他个人发展和苏联体系发展的关键转折点。对他而言，斯大林发起的净化政策说明了有必要开展类似的自我净化运动。

The Communist state, the play signals, does not crush all individuals, as Bobrov had feared. It invites into its collective fold everyone who demonstrates a sincere desire to become involved in the construction effort. Moreover, it breeds a generation of fearless, optimistic people who will inhabit the socialist home. Fear is felt only by those who situate themselves against history, who obstruct the construction: together with their useless belongings, they are swept away in the housecleaning and crushed, like useless cups of Sèvres china.

Afinogenov, when writing the play, did not foresee that in 1937 he himself would become the target of a purge as described in Fear. As the Stalinist Great Purge unfolded, engulfing the playwright along with thousands of others, he recorded his experience not in the form of a play, but in a personal diary—an intimate theater, as it were, in which he staged the drama of his life. Afinogenov, whose life during the 1930s is also richly documented by his plays, public appearances, and personal letters, viewed the purge that threatened him as a time of historical possibility. It was a moment when history breathed directly on him and when the drama of his life was elevated to a world-historical level. He saw the year 1937 as a critical juncture in both his personal development and the development of the Soviet system. For him, the policies of purification launched by Stalin illustrated the need to embark on a similar campaign of self-purification.

在某种程度上，阿菲诺格诺夫著作中生活与文本界限的反复模糊，是身为专业剧作家的表现，他情不自禁地用戏剧术语构思自己的人生。然而，更根本地说，它表达了一位苏联共产党人试图将其“主观”自我与“客观”现实相统一的尝试。在此，阿菲诺格诺夫作为剧作家的才华只是为他与同时代其他共产党员共同追求的目标赋予了更丰富的文学形式。按照文学-历史剧本组织起来，阿菲诺格诺夫的自我叙事让人想起列昂尼德·波特姆金的叙事，但这位剧作家的剧本在象征性行为方面比那位地质学学生走得远得多。两人都将自己视为肩负重大历史责任的“人类灵魂工程师”，作为一名共产主义鼓动者，波特姆金最多只与几百名学生观众打交道，而阿菲诺格诺夫的剧作则触及了数百万观众。植根于可追溯到19世纪批评家别林斯基和车尔尼雪夫斯基的传统，阿菲诺格诺夫知道，他作为向大众宣讲新历史生活形式的意识形态家所具有的神圣地位，只有当他亲自为新生活之路树立榜样时，才能有效和合法。

To some extent, the repeated blurring of the lines between life and text in Afinogenov’s writings was the work of a professional playwright who could not help conceiving of his life in dramaturgical terms. More fundamentally, however, it expressed a Soviet Communist’s attempts to align his “subjective” self with “objective” reality. Here Afinogenov’s talent as a playwright only lent richer literary form to a striving he shared with other Communists of his time. Organized according to a literary-historical script, Afinogenov’s self-narrative is reminiscent of Leonid Potemkin’s, but the playwright’s scenario vastly surpassed that of the geology student in symbolic behavior. Both men regarded themselves as “engineers of human souls” with great historical responsibilities, as a Communist agitator Potemkin worked with audiences of a few hundred students at best, while Afinogenov’s plays reached millions of spectators. Rooted in a tradition dating back to the nineteenth-century critics Belinsky and Chernyshevsky, Afinogenov knew that his priestly status as an ideologue who preached new historical life forms to his mass audience would be effective and legitimate only if he personally exemplified the path toward the new life.

然而，与革命前那些可以自由幻想完美未来及其居民的前辈不同，阿菲诺格诺夫则在共产主义国家的限制下工作，这个国家的领导人声称有权定义苏联秩序正在经历的历史发展阶段。作为一名共产主义剧作家，阿菲诺格诺夫有责任揭示历史走向完美未来的工作；然而，过去俄国作家所声称的历史立法者的角色现在落到了斯大林身上。阿菲诺格诺夫的日记在展示了在斯大林的监视下辨析历史在智力和审美上是多么艰巨的任务的同时，也表明他作为斯大林的作家这一职业提供了普通苏联公民无法获得的自我实现的可能性。

Unlike his prerevolutionary predecessors, however, who were free to fantasize about the perfect future and the type of people who would in-habit it, Afinogenov worked under the constraints of a Communist state whose leader claimed the authority to define the stages of historical development that the Soviet order was traversing. As a Communist playwright, Afinogenov had a responsibility to reveal the work of history toward the perfect future; yet the role of historical legislator claimed by Russian writers in the past now fell to Stalin. While showing how demanding a task it was, intellectually and aesthetically, to discern history under Stalin’s watchful eye, Afinogenov’s diary also shows that his vocation as Stalin’s writer provided possibilities of self-realization unavailable to ordinary Soviet citizens.

en: Engineer of Human Souls

children: 亚历山大·阿菲诺格诺夫于1904年出生在梁赞省的一个小镇。他的父亲是一名铁路工人，在他出生后不久就离开了家，去西伯利亚工作，并在那里开始了写作生涯。亚历山大由母亲抚养长大，母亲是一名乡村教师和当地报纸的兼职编辑。革命爆发后，13岁的亚历山大被选为当地共产主义学生联合会秘书。三年后，他加入了共产党，之后他在苏联政权中担任了六个不同的职务，包括军事审查员和报纸编辑。正如他在自传中回忆的那样：“我来到学校……用我盛气凌人的样子和腰带上的左轮手枪吓坏了老师。”
阿菲诺格诺夫于1927年搬到莫斯科，加入了当时最具影响力和激进的文学组织——俄罗斯无产阶级作家协会（RAPP）；他于1929年当选为该协会理事会成员。他的早期剧作《怪人》（1929年）和《恐惧》遵循了RAPP 所倡导的“无产阶级现实主义”美学，专注于苏联社会中的矛盾，而不寻求美化现实。
忠于这一指示，阿菲诺格诺夫毫不避讳地揭露共产党内个人的过失和行政缺陷。他的剧作广受欢迎，并受到共产主义领导人的赞扬。据报道，约瑟夫·斯大林在与其他政治局成员一起观看了《怪人》之后，“指示”中央委员会成员都去观看这部“非凡”且“必要”的剧作。
到20世纪30年代初，阿菲诺格诺夫开始与斯大林通信，他将斯大林视为他至高无上的文学导师，后来他还将剧作草稿提交给斯大林审查。阿菲诺格诺夫的一部关于红军指挥官生平的剧作，在其正式首演前，在国防人民委员克利门特·伏罗希洛夫的公寓里被朗读。另一位主要导师是马克西姆·高尔基。1932年春天，阿菲诺格诺夫在高尔基位于意大利的家中做客三周。

Alexander Afinogenov was born in 1904 in a small town in Riazan province. His father, a railroad employee, left the family soon after the boy’s birth to work in Siberia, where he started a writing career. Alexander was raised by his mother, a village schoolteacher and part-time editor of a local newspaper. After the outbreak of the revolution the 13-year-old Alexander was elected secretary of a local Union of Communist Students. Three years later he joined the Communist party, after which he worked for the Soviet regime in six different functions, including military censor and newspaper editor. As he remembered in an autobiography: “I came to school . . . and scared the teachers with my domineering appearance and the revolver attached to my belt.”

Afinogenov moved to Moscow in 1927 and joined the Russian Association of Proletarian Writers (RAPP), the most vocal and militant literary organization of the time; he was elected to its board of directors in 1929. His early plays, The Eccentric (1929) and Fear, followed the “proletarian realist” aesthetic advocated by RAPP, focusing on contradictions in Soviet society without seeking to embellish reality.

Faithful to this directive, Afinogenov did not refrain from exposing personal failures and administrative deficiencies within the Communist party. His plays were widely popular and received praise from Communist leaders. Joseph Stalin, after attending The Eccentric with other members of the Politburo, reportedly “prescribed” that members of the Central Committee go and see this “remarkable” and “necessary” play.

By the early 1930s Afinogenov was corresponding with Stalin, whom he regarded as his supreme literary mentor, and to whom he would later submit drafts of his plays for criticism. One of Afinogenov’s plays, about the life of a Red Army commander, was read before its official premiere in the apartment of the people’s commissar for defense, Kliment Voroshilov. Another chief mentor was Maxim Gorky. Afinogenov was a guest at Gorky’s house in Italy for three weeks in the spring of 1932.

阿菲诺格诺夫在苏联文学界的崛起，恰逢共产主义领导人以及高尔基努力将文学打造成为与社会主义时代黎明相称的独特“苏联”文化的首要传播媒介。1932年4月，一项党中央法令废除了所有现有文学组织，包括RAPP，并呼吁建立一个统一的苏联作家协会。此后，苏联文学将以统一的“社会主义现实主义”风格创作，以描绘并帮助实现新世界的到来。社会主义现实主义美学的关键在于艺术家对历史走向的正确把握。只有对这一进程具有卓越洞察力的艺术家才能胜任共产主义艺术家。正如中央委员会文学事务发言人安德烈·日丹诺夫所阐述的文学界面临的任务：“苏联文学必须能够……瞥见我们的明天。这不会是一个乌托邦，因为我们的明天正在今天的基础上通过有计划和自觉的工作进行准备……作家不能落后于事件，他必须站在人民的第一线，向人民展示其发展道路。”

斯大林亲自为苏联作家规定了他们的创作主题。1932年10月，他在马克西姆·高尔基位于莫斯科的寓所召集了一批作家，其中包括阿菲诺格诺夫；高尔基刚刚从意大利返回。斯大林呼吁苏联作家加入工业化运动，成为“人类灵魂工程师”。在工业化运动以惊人的速度重塑数百万公民的社会存在时，作家们则要帮助公民组织他们的内心生活。每个苏联读者或戏剧观众都应根据作家对社会主义英雄情感和思想世界的描绘来塑造自己。斯大林特别对在场的剧作家们说：“你们应该写什么？诗歌很好。小说更好。但现在最好的还是戏剧。戏剧容易理解……戏剧是我们最需要的一种艺术形式。工人可以轻松观看戏剧……资产阶级在早期产生了一些最伟大的戏剧天才，如莎士比亚、莫里哀，这并非偶然……我们必须创作自己的戏剧。”

Afinogenov’s rise to the apex of the Soviet literary establishment co-incided with the effort, on the part of Communist leaders as well as Gorky, to make literature the foremost medium for the propagation of a distinctly “Soviet” culture commensurate with the dawning socialist age. In April 1932 a party decree abolished all existing literary organizations, including RAPP, and called for the establishment of a single association of Soviet writers. Soviet literature was henceforth to be produced in a unified “socialist realist” style, to chart and help bring about the emerging new world. Key to the socialist realist aesthetic was the artist’s proper grasp of the direction in which history was traveling. Only artists with superior insight into this process could qualify as Communist artists. As Andrei Zhdanov, Central Committee spokesman on literary matters, formulated the task awaiting the writing profession: “Soviet literature must be able to . . . glimpse our tomorrow. This will not be a utopia, since our tomorrow is already being prepared today on the basis of planned and conscious work . . . The writer must not lag behind the events, he has to be among the first ranks of the people and show the people the path of its development.”

Stalin personally prescribed to Soviet writers the subject of their trade. In October 1932 he convened a group of writers, including Afinogenov, in the Moscow residence of Maxim Gorky, who had just returned from living in Italy. Stalin appealed to Soviet writers to join the industrialization campaign and become “engineers of human souls.” While the industrialization campaign recast the social existence of millions of citizens at breakneck speed, writers were to help citizens organize their inner lives. It was according to their portrayals of the socialist hero’s emotional-intellectual world that each Soviet reader or theatergoer was to mold himself. Stalin addressed the assembled playwrights in particular: “What should you write? Poetry is fine. Novels are even better. But plays are now best of all. Plays are easy to understand . . . Plays are the art form we need most of all. Workers can watch plays easily . . . It is no accident that the bourgeois class, at the outset, produced some of its greatest geniuses in drama: Shakespeare, Molière . . . We must make our own plays.”
阿菲诺格诺夫在这次会议后被任命为筹备苏联作家联盟成立大会的委员会成员，他以字面意义上的方式遵循了斯大林的要求。他在1933年至1936年期间的公开声明呼吁描绘新人丰富的心理世界，正如阿菲诺格诺夫所定义的“灵魂”。

然而，这种方法仍然存在争议。弗谢沃洛德·维什涅夫斯基和尼古拉·波戈金，两位同行剧作家，攻击阿菲诺格诺夫过分强调人物的内心生活，在他们看来，这带有“反动”传统主义的色彩。相反，他们主张一种充满戏剧动作的宏伟风格；他们力求突出英雄群体，而不是孤立的个体。从本质上讲，这两个阵营在什么更适合苏联读者和观众的问题上存在分歧：是突出新人内心心理冲突并展示解决途径的文学；还是通过完美未来的投射来动员读者和观众的宏大场景。

这场辩论的所有参与者都辩称他们的立场是“正确”执行党的任务，即创作与新兴社会主义时代相称的艺术。他们紧抓斯大林、日丹诺夫和其他领导人发布的规定性声明和指示，作为他们立场的授权。但这些授权姿态只是掩盖了这样一个事实：归根结底，并没有明确的指示说明社会主义现实主义“方法”究竟是什么——它预见什么样的情节结构，应如何权衡不完美的当下与完美的未来各自所占的分量，以及一个剧本在描绘通往未来的斗争时可以有多少冲突和矛盾。辩论的参与者们仍需将他们所认为的新美学敏感性的关键原则付诸实践。他们所从事的是一项实验性的、往往相当冒险的追求。

Afinogenov, who after this meeting was appointed to the committee that organized the founding congress of the Union of Soviet Writers, followed Stalin’s demand in literal fashion. His public statements of the period 1933–1936 called for portrayals of the new man’s rich psychological world, as Afinogenov defined the term “soul.”

Yet this approach remained controversial. Vsevolod Vishnevsky and Nikolai Pogodin, two fellow playwrights, attacked Afinogenov for his emphasis on characters’ inner lives, which in their eyes smacked of “re-actionary” traditionalism. Instead they advocated a monumental style saturated with dramatic action; they sought to foreground heroic masses, not isolated individuals. Essentially the two camps disagreed over what served Soviet readers and spectators better: literature that highlighted psychological conflicts within the new man while showing ways to resolve them; or epic scenarios that mobilized readers and viewers through the projection of the perfect future.

All participants in this debate defended their positions as the “correct” implementation of the party mandate to produce art commensurate with the emerging socialist age. They clung to prescriptive statements and signals issued by Stalin, Zhdanov, and other leaders as authorizations of their positions. But these authorizing gestures only masked the fact that at bottom there was no clear indication of what a socialist realist “method” amounted to—what kind of plot structure it foresaw, what relative  weight was to be given to the imperfect present and the perfect future, and how much conflict and ambivalence a script could have in its depiction of the struggle toward the future. It remained for the participants in the debate to put into practice what they saw as the key principles of the new aesthetic sensibility. Theirs was an experimental and often quite risky pursuit.

阿菲诺格诺夫心理学方法的争议性，在1933年秋季首演的剧作《谎言》所受到的反响中凸显出来。该剧创作于从“无产阶级”现实主义转向“社会主义”现实主义，从描绘当下缺陷到展望完美未来的关键时刻，其倾向性批判多于乐观。秉承阿菲诺格诺夫以往作品的传统，该剧沉浸于模糊性之中，描绘了年轻共产党员妮娜不稳定的世界观。妮娜被另一位党员引诱，后者在她不知情的情况下正在策划反革命，使她相信苏联是一个充满谎言和欺骗的国家。最终，一位成熟的共产党员将这位陷入困境的女主人公从她危险的政治关系中解救出来。高尔基和斯大林，阿菲诺格诺夫曾向他们寄送了剧本副本，都猛烈抨击其歪曲共产党。正如高尔基所观察到的，剧中大多数共产党员角色肤浅且描绘得灰暗，与对其敌人的生动刻画形成对比。高尔基说，尽管自己不是党员，却能辨认出布尔什维克的人格。“布尔什维克有趣之处不在于他的缺点，”他教导阿菲诺格诺夫，“而在于他的优点。他的缺点根植于他正不倦摧毁的过去。然而，他的优点根植于现在，根植于建设未来的工作中……我们必须训练自己，从我们未来目标的角度来评价过去和现在。”

The controversial nature of Afinogenov’s psychological approach came to the fore in the reception of his play Lie, which premiered in the fall of 1933. Written at the very juncture of the shift from “proletarian” to “socialist” realism, from accounts of present-day deficiencies to projections of the perfect future, the play had a more critical than optimistic bent. In the tradition of Afinogenov’s previous work, it reveled in ambiguity, portraying the unsteady worldview of a young Communist, Nina. Nina is lured by an another party member, who unbeknownst to her is plotting a counterrevolution, into believing that the Soviet Union is a country of lies and deceit. In the end a mature Communist rescues the entangled heroine from her dangerous political liaison. Both Gorky and Stalin, to whom Afinogenov sent copies of the script, slammed it for distorting the Communist party. As Gorky observed, most of the Communist characters in the play were shallow and rendered in shades of gray, in contrast to the lively portrayal of their foes. Even though he, Gorky, was not a party member, he could recognize a Bolshevik’s personality. “A Bolshevik is interesting not for his faults,” he lectured Afinogenov, “but for his virtues. His faults are rooted in the past which he is tirelessly destroying. His virtues, however, are rooted in the present, in the work of building the future . . . We have to train ourselves to appraise the past and the present from the vantage point of our future goals.”

阿菲诺格诺夫的最高批评者斯大林，其反应甚至比高尔基更加负面。他质问道，为什么剧中没有坚定的共产党员，“真诚无私，全心全意投身于工人事业”？“睁开你的眼睛，你会看到党内有这样的工人。”在妮娜承认社会主义正在建设，但代价是如此冷漠，以至于当电车轧过一个女人时，旁观者只是诅咒交通延误的一段文字旁，斯大林讽刺地批注道“哈——哈——哈”。他划掉了剧本接近结尾处的一整个段落，其中妮娜承认她和其他年轻共产党员已经失去了对革命的献身精神：“我们不知道[党的]总路线明天会是什么。今天它被称为路线，明天就成了偏差。报纸也不写出全部真相。我厌倦了这样的生活。”“谁需要这种沉闷无聊的胡言乱语？”斯大林评论道。在附带的批注中，他认可了阿菲诺格诺夫创作该剧的想法，但建议进行重大修改。剧作家重新修改了《谎言》，该剧以修订后的形式在哈尔科夫的一家剧院首演，并受到热烈欢迎。另有三百家苏联剧院也签约制作该剧，其中包括几家莫斯科主要剧院。但在莫斯科首演预定日期前几天，斯大林再次表达了他的不赞成。阿菲诺格诺夫立即向各剧院发出电报，命令将《谎言》从剧目中撤下。

在他的批评者看来，阿菲诺格诺夫未能满足社会主义现实主义的要求。他的剧作没有展现支撑苏联领导人对实现完美未来信念的坚定且发展成熟的共产主义意志，反而播下了混乱和怀疑的种子。鉴于他对共产主义主人公的偏颇描绘，高尔基和斯大林甚至怀疑阿菲诺格诺夫是否真心是一个布尔什维克。这种指责，即尽管他是共产党员，阿菲诺格诺夫的剧作却只是“从外部”并通过“扭曲的镜子”展现苏联现实，在接下来的几年里不断出现在官方评论中。

Afinogenov’s supreme critic, Stalin, reacted even more negatively than Gorky. Why, he demanded, were there no committed Communists in the play, “sincere and unselfish, devoted heart and soul to the workers’ cause”? “Open your eyes and you will see that we have such workers in the party.” In the margin of a passage where Nina acknowledges that socialism is being built, but at the price of such indifference that when a streetcar runs over a woman the bystanders merely curse the traffic delay, Stalin noted a sarcastic “ha—ha—ha.” He crossed out an entire section toward the end of the play where Nina confesses that she and other young Communists have lost their revolutionary commitment: “We don’t know what the [party’s] general line will be tomorrow. Today it is called the line, tomorrow a deviation. And the newspapers don’t write the whole truth. I’m tired of living like this.” “Who needs this dismal and tedious gibberish?” Stalin commented. In an accompanying note he endorsed Afinogenov’s idea for the play but recommended major revisions. The playwright reworked Lie, which premiered in revised form at a theater in Kharkov and was received enthusiastically. Three hundred other Soviet theaters also contracted to produce the play, among them several leading Moscow houses. But a few days before the scheduled Moscow premiere, Stalin again voiced his disapproval. Immediately Afinogenov sent telegrams to the theaters ordering Lie to be withdrawn from the repertoire.

In the eyes of his critics, Afinogenov had failed to meet the demands of socialist realism. Instead of showcasing the firm and developed Communist will that underpinned Soviet leaders’ trust that the perfect future would be attained, his play sowed confusion and doubt. Given his skewed portrayal of Communist protagonists, Gorky and Stalin even doubted whether Afinogenov was a true Bolshevik at heart. This reproach that, despite his membership in the Communist party, Afinogenov’s plays showed Soviet reality only “from the outside” and through a “distorted mirror,” was repeated in official reviews over the next years.

高尔基和斯大林对《谎言》的批评在阿菲诺格诺夫的朋友、演员鲍里斯·伊格里茨基的一次私人评价中得到了呼应。伊格里茨基在他的日记中评论该剧的失败时，将其归因于阿菲诺格诺夫过于狭隘的生活经验。“亚历山大没有经历过内战的洗礼，也没有参与经济建设工作，他没有深入工人文化，也没有深入乡村生活。他从未从内心深处被我们党的热情感染，从未被党的‘狂飙突进’所吸引，也从未被卷入其中。”伊格里茨基也怀疑阿菲诺格诺夫的布尔什维克资格，暗示他的作品的不足表达了他缺乏政治意识。围绕这一主题，伊格里茨基指责阿菲诺格诺夫没有过上一个共产党员应有的生活。一次对阿菲诺格诺夫莫斯科新公寓的拜访——日记作者指出，这套公寓花费了两万卢布——让伊格里茨基深刻认识到这位剧作家很少参与苏联集体的困苦或热情：“一个宽敞、独立的四居室公寓，很多家具，枝形吊灯，各种物品。一切都是新的，都很昂贵……一切都多么舒适，多么舒适而空虚！我跟他在一起感到很难过。一个独自工作的工匠，从整体中分离出来的一块。”伊格里茨基将阿菲诺格诺夫被察觉到的艺术缺陷归因于他道德人格上的缺陷。在他的朋友看来，阿菲诺格诺夫在苏联事业中扎根不够深。

Gorky’s and Stalin’s criticisms of Lie were echoed in a private evaluation by a friend of Afinogenov’s, the actor Boris Igritsky. Commenting in his diary on the failure of the play, Igritsky attributed it to Afinogenov’s overly narrow life experience. “Alexander did not go through the school of the civil war and did not take part in the economic construction work, he did not become deeply absorbed in workers’ culture, nor in village life. He was never organically infected with the passions of our party and never got carried away by the party’s Sturm und Drang, nor was he drawn into them.” Igritsky, too, doubted Afinogenov’s Bolshevik credentials, implying that the shortcomings of his oeuvre expressed his lack of political consciousness. Expanding on this theme, Igritsky accused Afinogenov of not leading a life worthy of a Communist. A visit to Afinogenov’s new Moscow apartment—which, the diarist noted, had cost twenty thousand rubles—underscored for Igritsky how little the playwright partook in either the deprivations or the enthusiasms of the Soviet collective: “A large, separate four-room apartment, lots of furniture, chandeliers, things. Everything new and expensive . . . How comfortable everything is, how cozy and empty! I felt sad being with him. A craftsman working alone, a piece broken off from the whole.” Igritsky attributed Afinogenov’s perceived artistic deficiencies to a defect in his moral personality. In his friend’s eyes, Afinogenov was not sufficiently rooted in the Soviet cause.

阿菲诺格诺夫确实富裕，而且不仅仅是按照苏联标准而言。他月收入14,000卢布，而苏联工人的平均月收入是几百卢布。他可以使用专为共产党精英保留的特供商店，并被允许出国旅行。在1932年春夏季进行了一次漫长的欧洲之旅后，阿菲诺格诺夫乘坐他的新车——一辆福特——回到了俄罗斯。他与戏剧界的朋友们一起在克里米亚和黑海沿岸的部长级别墅度假。剧院导演尼古拉·彼得罗夫的日记记录了他与阿菲诺格诺夫及其他人度假时玩的扑克牌游戏。在这些游戏中，数以百计的卢布在牌桌上易手，其中包括一种未指明的“狂野亚洲扑克”。增加阿菲诺格诺夫魅力的是他与一位美国芭蕾舞演员兼共产党员的婚姻，他于1920年代末在莫斯科认识了她。也多亏了他的妻子珍妮，阿菲诺格诺夫经常作为美国大使在莫斯科举办的招待会的座上宾。根据另一位朋友鲍里斯·帕斯捷尔纳克的说法，阿菲诺格诺夫“被莫斯科一半的艺术界人士包围着。”
这位剧作家是佩列德尔基诺作家村的首批居民之一，该村位于首都以西十五英里。这个作家村由国家建立的昂贵别墅组成，旨在为杰出的作家们创造最佳的创作条件。正是在佩列德尔基诺，阿菲诺格诺夫的人生戏剧将在1937年上演。

Afinogenov was indeed affluent, and not just by Soviet standards. He drew a monthly income of 14,000 rubles, whereas the average income for Soviet workers was a few hundred rubles. He had access to special shops reserved for the Communist elite and was allowed to travel abroad. After an extended trip to Europe in the spring and summer of 1932, Afinogenov returned to Russia in his new car, a Ford. Together with friends from the theater world he vacationed in ministerial dachas in the Crimea and on the Black Sea coast. The diary of the theater director Nikolai Petrov records the poker games he played with Afinogenov and others while on vacation. Hundreds of rubles crossed the table during these games, which included an unspecified variant of “wild Asian poker.” Adding to Afinogenov’s appeal was his marriage to an American ballerina—and Communist—whom he had met in Moscow in the late 1920s. Thanks also to his wife, Jenny, Afinogenov was a regular guest at receptions in Moscow given by the American ambassador. According to Boris Pasternak, another friend, Afinogenov was  “surrounded by half of Moscow’s art world.”

The playwright was among the first residents of the writers’ colony of Peredelkino, a village fifteen miles west of the capital. The colony consisted of expensive dachas set up by the state to create the best conditions for its outstanding writers to pursue their trade. It was in Peredelkino that the drama of Afinogenov’s life would play itself out in 1937.

en: Gymnastics of the Soul

children: 阿菲诺格诺夫的日记揭示，他与他的朋友伊格里茨基一样，将《谎言》的失败解释为他个人失败的体现。阿菲诺格诺夫于1926年开始写日记，并坚持了一生。除了1936年至1938年期间，他的日记只以片段形式存世——大部分是未注明日期的打字纸片，没有清晰的顺序。原本连贯的日记被阿菲诺格诺夫自己剪散：在准备他的剧本时，他反复用剪刀翻阅日记，剪下段落并按主题整理。这个习惯为日记的一个主要功能提供了线索：作为他文学作品的速写本。在大多数情况下，日记条目充满了阿菲诺格诺夫日常生活的观察：家中的对话和与同事的交流，街头景象，对自然、人类心理和政治生活的思考。

这个速写本的一个显著特点是它的自省性质。阿菲诺格诺夫的自我观察与他作为共产主义作家的使命紧密相连。他实践着一个可追溯到19世纪评论家车尔尼雪夫斯基的道德使命，根据该使命，作家必须亲自体现他所宣扬的革命标准。对阿菲诺格诺夫来说，这意味着，要成为一名合格的灵魂工程师，他必须塑造自己的灵魂。他对新人的内心生活的描绘，只有作为他个人感受到的意识的投射才能成功。作家必须“将他的灵魂投入到他的作品中，”他在他的日记中写道。写作应该是“写自己，[作家]自身‘自我’的主题。”

社会主义现实主义要求艺术家揭示所考察对象与历史进程的关系。在阿菲诺格诺夫的例子中，要考察的对象是他的灵魂。写日记是为了帮助他观察自己。在日记中提及自己时，阿菲诺格诺夫通常使用第三人称。他在日记页面上观察自己，仿佛他是一个舞台上的角色。鉴于日记作为他作品素材库的功能，这很有道理：在日记中，自传性的“他”和他的剧本角色在同一层面上移动并变得可以互换。这也意味着，无论是按社会主义现实主义方式构思的舞台人物，还是日记中的“他”，都必须符合模范革命生活的同一标准。

Afinogenov’s diary reveals that he, like his friend Igritsky, interpreted the failure of Lie as related to his failure as a person. Afinogenov began to keep a diary in 1926 and did so for the rest of his life. Except for the period from 1936 to 1938, his diary survives only in fragments—scraps of mostly undated typewritten sheets without a clear sequence. The originally cohesive diary was torn apart by Afinogenov himself: in preparing his plays, he repeatedly went through his diary with scissors, cutting out passages and arranging them thematically. This habit provides a clue to a principal function of the diary: to serve as a sketchbook for his literary work. For the most part, diary entries abound in observations of Afinogenov’s daily life: conversations at home and with colleagues, street scenes, thoughts on nature, human psychology, and political life.

A striking feature of this sketchbook is its self-reflective quality. Afinogenov’s self-observation was tied to his calling as a Communist writer. He practiced a moral mandate dating back to the nineteenth-century critic Chernyshevsky, according to which a writer had to personally embody the revolutionary standards that he preached. For Afinogenov this meant that, to be a worthy engineer of souls, he must engineer his own soul. His portrayal of the new man’s interior life could only succeed as a projection of a consciousness that he personally felt. The writer must “invest his soul in his works,” he noted in his diary. Writing should be “writing about the self, the theme of the [writer’s] own ‘self.’”

Socialist realism required the artist to bring out the relationship of the object under investigation to the course of history. In Afinogenov’s case, the object to be investigated was his own soul. Keeping the diary was to help him observe himself. When referring to himself in the diary, Afinogenov usually used the third person. He observed himself on the pages of his journal as if he was a character on a stage. Given the diary’s function as a quarry for his works, this made sense: in the diary the autobiographical “he” and the characters of his plays moved on the same level and became interchangeable. This also meant that both the stage characters, conceived of in socialist realist fashion, and the diaristic “he” were subject to the same standard of an exemplary revolutionary life.

阿菲诺格诺夫的日记式自我分析向他揭示了其灵魂的腐败。他早期剧作的成功给他带来了名声，并鼓励他沉溺于生活的享乐之中。结果，他变得懒惰和自满，停止了斗争。在1935年元旦，回首过去的一年，他写道：“困惑、沮丧，……以及对自我的探寻，在持续的不确定中……而现在才突然明白，我不能再这样生活下去了。”一年后，在1935年12月末，他写道：“什么都没真正做成，这一年都在消耗前一年取得的成果……这不是寄生虫行为吗？”
这种空虚和停滞预示着堕落，因为成为一名共产党员意味着在不断的斗争中前进，与历史不可阻挡的进程保持一致。阿菲诺格诺夫在此期间写的一篇未注明日期的笔记，题为《分离》，暗示了他的危机程度。这篇笔记是关于珍妮的，她在发现了他写给一位年轻女演员的情书后，刚刚离开他回到了美国。阿菲诺格诺夫以严厉的自责口吻回忆起她离开那天他站在她身边，但在内心深处却感觉与她相隔千里：
他除了围绕自己的种种盘算和怨叹，什么也感觉不到。一个渺小的利己主义者和麻木不仁的人。他亲爱的、曾经亲密的伴侣，为他做了那么多，培养了他的品格和意志，他的妻子常常为她的劳动成果感到骄傲，她就是从一个意志薄弱、精神萎靡的男孩手中培养出这种男人。但两年时间——所有这些培养都像蒲公英一样被风吹散了，他又回到了老路，她不得不一切从头再来。

Afinogenov’s diaristic self-analysis disclosed to him a corruption of his soul. The success of his early plays had brought him fame and encouraged him to indulge in the pleasures of life. As a result, he had turned lazy and complacent and stopped struggling. On New Year’s Day 1935, looking back on the past year, he wrote: “Confusion, depression, . . . and the search for myself, in constant uncertainty . . . And only now has it suddenly become clear that I can’t go on living like this.” A year later, in late December 1935, he noted: “Nothing real has been done, the year was spent at the expense of what had been done the previous year . . . Isn’t that parasitism?”

This emptiness and lack of movement signaled degeneration, for to be a Communist meant to be moving ahead in constant struggle, in tune with the inexorable march of history. An undated note by Afinogenov from this period, entitled “The Separation,” suggests the extent of his crisis. It was about Jenny, who had just left him and returned to the United States after discovering his love letters to a young actress. In harshly self-accusatory terms Afinogenov recalled standing next to her the day she left, but feeling in-ternally miles apart from her:

He didn’t feel anything except all sorts of rooting around and moaning concerning himself. A petty egoist and callous person. His dear, at one time intimate companion, who had done so much for him, nurturing his character and will, his wife often took pride in the fruits of her labor, here’s the sort of man that she has reared from a weak-willed and low-spirited boy. But in two years’ time—all this nurturing was blown away, like a dandelion, he drifted to the old ways, and she had to begin everything all over again.
阿菲诺格诺夫的自我评价呼应了鲍里斯·伊格里茨基对他朋友粗心大意、被宠坏、十足“妈宝男”的判断。但阿菲诺格诺夫的笔记也表明他多么沉浸于一种批判性自我分析的文化中，并且他将他的妻子，以及像伊格里茨基这样的朋友，视为倾诉和忏悔的对象，他们要提供他自己所缺乏的坚定性。（珍妮后来回到了她的丈夫身边；时间不详。）

在这种背景下，阿菲诺格诺夫将他的日记视为重新获得作为灵魂工程师职业所必需的纪律和奉献精神的途径。他将写日记设想为一种共产主义自我的技术。写日记使得一个持续的自我剖析和净化过程成为可能，阿菲诺格诺夫将其比作祈祷的结果：“祈祷的意义——来临之日前的洁净。净化灵魂。这根本没那么愚蠢，当然，不是以死记硬背的祈祷形式，而是像这样：反思未来的一天和过去的一天……灵魂的体操。”阿菲诺格诺夫众多自我提升的呼吁之一被表述为一种祈祷：“好吧，利用它……在未来十年里展现你自己……以至于没有一天被浪费，没有一小时被花在奢靡或狂欢上……对自己要求更高！学会批评自己，这样别人就会少批评你……学会希望并相信自己……阿门。”

Afinogenov’s self-characterization echoed Boris Igritsky’s judgment that his friend was careless and spoiled, a true “mama’s boy.” But Afinogenov’s note also suggests how steeped he was in a culture of critical self-analysis, and that he viewed his wife, and also friends like Igritsky, as confessors who were to provide the steadfastness that he himself lacked. (Jenny later returned to her husband; it is unclear when.)

In this context Afinogenov viewed his diary as a means to regain the discipline and dedication essential to his vocation as an engineer of souls. He conceived of writing the diary as a technology of the Communist self. Keeping the diary made possible a continuous process of baring and cleansing the self, which Afinogenov likened to the results of prayer: “The significance of prayer—the cleansing before the coming day. Cleansing the soul. This is not that stupid at all, of course, not in the form of a prayer learned by rote, but like this: to reflect on the day to come as well as on the past day . . . gymnastics for the soul.” One of Afinogenov’s many appeals for self-improvement was formulated as a prayer: “Well, make use of it . . . show yourself over the next ten years . . . in such a way that not a single day is wasted and not a single hour is spent on extravagance or revelry . . . Demand more of yourself! Learn to criticize yourself, so that others will criticize you less . . . Learn to hope and to believe in yourself . . . Amen.”

阿菲诺格诺夫刻意使用宗教习语来描述他的自我改造工作。正如他反复指出的，新的社会主义社会虽然拥有灵魂的语言，但缺乏激发公民培养灵魂纯洁性的制度和机制，而苏联制度的力量最终就建立在灵魂的纯洁性之上。苏联政治根本不涵盖日常伦理领域，而宗教，作为压迫工具被正确揭露，当然也不是替代方案。作家的任务是介入并提供精神指导，帮助读者度过危机并恢复他们的社会承诺。阿菲诺格诺夫将苏联剧院比作一座教堂：“人们必须去那里学习如何生活和行为，当你聆听舞台上的言语时，将它们应用于你自己，以及你与远近朋友、敌人、陌生人和家人的关系。”
然而，一个根本问题仍然存在：如果剧作家自己缺乏精神上的坚韧，他又如何能履行他的神圣职责呢？阿菲诺格诺夫在1935年日记中勾勒的一部小说大纲中描述了他的危机。这是一部他“必须不考虑任何可能因伦理或政治原因而被删除的内容”来写的小说，换句话说，他知道这部小说无法通过他的文学审查员斯大林的审查：

我必须写一个关于“无”的简单故事，关于一个无法确定自己是谁的人的思想和行动……并且以这样一种方式来写：不包含任何数字，不包含任何关于第二个五年计划的统计数据，就像这个人生活在一个岛上，仅仅出于习惯阅读报纸，又出于同样的习惯忘记他读过的所有东西一样简单。一个关于生活成为习惯以及以英雄方式改造自己的困难的故事。这本书将是关于许多人的，而且，是我们都认识的人……一部没有主题，没有目标的小说：他只是起床，环顾四周，然后明白他生活得很糟糕。但他无法向自己解释为什么他生活得很糟糕。

Afinogenov deliberately used the religious idiom to describe his work of self-transformation. As he noted repeatedly, the new socialist society, while possessing a language of the soul, lacked institutions and mechanisms that incited citizens to cultivate the purity of their souls, on which the strength of the Soviet system ultimately rested. Soviet politics simply did not cover the area of everyday ethics, and religion, rightly exposed as an instrument of oppression, was of course no alternative. It was the task of the writer to step in and provide spiritual guidance to help readers work through crises and restore their social commitments. Afinogenov likened the Soviet theater to a church: “One must go there to learn how to live and behave, and as you listen to the words on the stage, apply them to yourself and to your relations with friends both near and far away, enemies, strangers, and family.”

Yet there remained a fundamental problem: How could the playwright perform his priestly calling if he himself lacked spiritual fortitude? Afinogenov described his crisis in the outline of a novel that he sketched out in his diary in 1935. It was a novel he had “to write without any consideration of what might be crossed out on ethical or political grounds,” a novel, in other words, that he knew would not pass the desk of his literary censor, Stalin:

I must write a simple story about nothing, about the thoughts and the actions of a person who can’t determine who he is . . . And write it in such a way that there won’t be any numbers, nor any statistics about the Second Five-Year Plan, as simply as if this person were living on an island, reading the newspapers out of sheer habit, and by this same habit forgetting everything he’s read. A story about life becoming a habit and the difficulty of making oneself over in a heroic fashion. This book will be about many people, moreover, people whom we all know . . . a novel without a theme, without a goal: he simply gets up, looks around, and understands that he is living poorly. But he can’t explain to himself why he is living poorly.

主人公，一位作家，过得不好是因为他感受不到他那个时代的宏伟。他机械地阅读报纸，而不是怀着真诚的奉献精神。他的灵魂是空虚的，缺乏将苏联报纸上刊载的指示和图表转化为即将到来的完美未来愿景所需的热情。他的危机是信仰的失落，苏联共产党人将其表达为历史确定性的丧失。主人公的病态源于他与自己曾经融为一体的集体脱离。尽管无法感受到远处真实的“生活”，他却知道它“正大踏步前进”。这个文学上的反英雄人物是以《谎言》中那个怀疑的共产党员妮娜为原型的。相比之下，他无法联系的理想是《恐惧》主人公叶莲娜所体现的坚强意志、革命热情和青春。

The protagonist, a writer, was not well because he could not feel the grandeur of his age. He read the newspaper mechanically, not with genuine dedication. His soul was empty, void of the fervent enthusiasm required to translate the directives and charts printed in Soviet newspapers into visions of an imminent perfect future. His crisis was a loss of faith, which Soviet Communists expressed as a loss of historical certainty. The hero’s sickness resulted from his dissociation from the collective of which he had once been an organic part. While unable to feel the real “life” somewhere in the distance, he knew that it was “making gigantic strides.” This literary antihero was patterned on Nina, the doubting Communist in Lie. By contrast, the ideal to which he was unable to connect was the strength of mind, revolutionary fervor, and youth embodied by Elena, the protagonist of Fear.

值得注意的是，这部未来的小说是关于“许多人……我们都认识的人”的。它涉及了苏联“创造性知识分子”的普遍危机。除了巨大的特权，阿菲诺格诺夫和他的同事们还肩负着书写时代历史的同样巨大的责任。斯大林的灵魂工程师们被苏联媒体的呼吁轰炸，例如《真理报》的这则呼吁：“数百万读者和观众渴望最高级的艺术形象；他们热切期待着他们的人生和斗争，我们这个世纪的伟大思想和事迹，能在充满力量和激情的艺术作品中展现，这些作品将载入社会主义文化史册，充实和组织不仅是同时代人，也是未来几代的思想和情感。”这些期望是如此之重，以至于伊萨克·巴别尔在作家大会上的讲话中说，它们简直让他作为一个作家噤声了。这番话半是玩笑，半是认真。

Significantly, this prospective novel was about “many people . . . whom we all know.” It addressed the crisis of the Soviet “creative intelligentsia” at large. Along with their enormous privileges, Afinogenov and his colleagues held the equally enormous responsibility of writing the history of the age. Stalin’s engineers of souls were bombarded with calls in the Soviet media, such as this appeal by Pravda: “Millions of readers and viewers want the highest images of art; they avidly wait for their life and struggle, for the great ideas and deeds of our century to be shown in artistic works of great force and passion, in works that will enter the history of socialist culture, filling and organizing the thoughts and feelings not only of contemporaries but of future generations.” So overwhelming were these expectations, Isaak Babel said in his address to the Writers’ Congress, that they simply silenced him as a writer. It was a remark made only half in jest.

阿菲诺格诺夫的回应则不同。无论是在作家大会上，还是在他的日记中，他都不断敦促自己和同事们将自己重塑为新人的典范，以不负他们的使命。但他们的困境在于，他们舒适特权的生活使他们与记录和综合在苏联建筑工地、煤矿、极地海域的浮冰上以及平流层中展开的真实历史生活的任务疏远了。这个问题显而易见。在1936年第十届共青团代表大会上，这预示着新一代纯洁的苏联青年出现，演讲者一个接一个地谴责“一些”作家在作为灵魂工程师的职责上“落后了”。原因被认定为他们的“肥胖……他们放弃了斗争。”

在阿菲诺格诺夫的日记、他与朋友的通信以及1930年代中期的公开声明中，可以感受到一种深刻的历史危机感。他将其描述为一种加速自我改造工作的冲动，以便与历史保持同步。历史正快速前进；新一代即将进入政治和文化生活，而他却在变老（1934年他才30岁），变得更加自满，身体也更重了。这是一种焦虑，他的自我与历史进程之间产生了鸿沟，而且这道鸿沟正变得越来越宽。这发生在一个任务是描绘历史道路的作家身上。阿菲诺格诺夫向尼古拉·彼得罗夫倾诉了这种焦虑，他还在作家大会上以更低调的语气表达了这一点。他宣称，作家不应专注于新人与旧过去之间的冲突；当下决定性的冲突在新人的内心展开。这是新人“对自己与国家赋予他的任务之间关系的不满，他对……自己的成长与国家整体成长之间关系的不满。”
阿菲诺格诺夫渴望与历史的共鸣。他揭示历史规律并使自己与历史进步进程保持一致的能力，是衡量他布尔什维克精神纯洁性的决定性标准。只有与历史同行，并在历史之中，他才能实现自己作为一个共产党员和作家的价值。因此，他渴望观察周围的“历史时代”、“事件”和“转折”；也因此，他焦虑历史进程可能会将他抛在身后，或者更糟的是，他可能会失去及时回身、把自己转变为历史主体的意志。

Afinogenov responded differently. Whether at the Writers’ Congress or in his diary, he kept urging himself as well as his colleagues to remake themselves into exemplars of the new man in order to live up to their calling. But their dilemma was that their comfortable lives of privilege estranged them from their task of recording and synthesizing the real, historical life that unfolded on Soviet construction sites and in coal mines, on ice floes in the polar sea, and in the stratosphere. The problem was in plain view. At the Tenth Komsomol Congress in 1936, which heralded the appearance of a new generation of untainted Soviet youth, speaker after speaker denounced “some” writers for “lagging behind” in their vocation as engineers of souls. The cause was identified as their “obesity . . . their abandonment of struggle.”

A profound sense of historical crisis is palpable in Afinogenov’s diary, his correspondence with friends, and his public statements of the mid-1930s. He described it as an urge to accelerate work on himself so as to remain in step with history. History was moving ahead at a rapid pace; a new generation was about to enter political and cultural life, while he was growing older (he was only 30 in 1934), more complacent, and physically heavier. It was an anxiety that a gap had formed between his self and the course of history, and that it was becoming ever wider. This was happening to a writer whose task was to chart the road of history. Afinogenov confided this anxiety to Nikolai Petrov, and he also stated it in more muted tones at the Writers’ Congress. Writers, he declared, should not focus on the conflict between the new man and an old past; the decisive conflict of the present played itself out within the new man. It was the new man’s “dissatisfaction with himself in relationship to the tasks posed to him by the country, his dissatisfaction . . . with his growth in relation to the overall growth of the country.”

Afinogenov craved a sense of communion with history. His ability to reveal the laws of history and to align himself in its progressive march was the decisive measure of the purity of his Bolshevik spirit. Only with, and in, history could he realize himself as a Communist individual and writer. Hence his yearning to observe “historical epochs,” “events,” and “turns” around him; hence also his anxiety that the course of history might pass him by or, even worse, that he might lose the will to turn in his tracks and transform himself into a subject of history.

children: 正是带着这种历史情怀，这位剧作家步入了1937年，这一年将毁掉数千名高级共产党员以及更多普通苏联公民的生活。在1936年期间，阿菲诺格诺夫面临着日益增多的官方批评。他首次在三月因反对形式主义的运动而受到训斥。同年晚些时候，他的剧作《万岁，西班牙！》在莫斯科首演。即时反响是积极的。《真理报》赞许地报道说，该剧演出赢得了起立鼓掌，并强调了该剧对来访的西班牙士兵代表团的强大影响。然而，仅仅几天后，在斯大林和其他布尔什维克领导人观看了一场演出后，《万岁，西班牙！》以及阿菲诺格诺夫的所有其他剧作突然从苏联剧院的剧目中撤下。阿菲诺格诺夫在1937年1月初告诉一位朋友，他预感到新年将给他的存在带来根本性挑战：“第一次”他面对“我生命、我的运动和我的命运的根本问题。”他再也无法忽视他生活中不利的结果：“我活得太久，却成就太少！”

It was with this historical disposition that the playwright entered the year 1937, which would devastate the lives of thousands of high-ranking Communists and an even larger number of less prominent Soviet citizens. Over the course of 1936 Afinogenov faced an increasing barrage of official criticism. He first received a reprimand in March in connection with the campaign against formalism. Later in the year his play Hail, Spain! premiered in Moscow. The immediate response was favorable. Pravda wrote approvingly that the performance elicited standing ovations, and emphasized the play’s powerful effect on a delegation of visiting Spanish soldiers. Only a few days later, however, after Stalin and other Bolshevik leaders had seen a performance, Hail, Spain! as well as all other plays by Afinogenov were suddenly withdrawn from the repertoire of Soviet theaters. Afinogenov told a friend in early January 1937 that he had a premonition that the new year would bring a fundamental challenge to his existence: “for the first time” he was confronted “with fundamental questions of my life, my movement, and my fate.” He could no longer ignore the unfavorable results of his life: “I have lived too long and achieved too little!”
在决定个人生活发生转折的同时，他在日记中指出，整个苏联体系同样也站在了一个十字路口。1936年11月，第八次苏维埃代表大会批准了新的苏联宪法

，该宪法被官方誉为世界上最民主的宪法。除其他公民权利外，宪法还规定以无记名投票选举所有国家代表机构，包括新成立的最高苏维埃。最高苏维埃的首次选举定于1937年末举行。在宪法批准后的几个月里，苏联媒体宣传了几项中央委员会决议，这些决议呼吁在即将到来的选举活动中实行更民主的程序，并告诫普通党员要对他们的当地领导人的表现更具批判性。《真理报》在1937年3月和4月报道，在地方选举中引入无记名投票后，许多在职官员在投票中落选。阿菲诺格诺夫对1937年初莫斯科党组织会议上弥漫的自我批评的质量印象深刻。在他关于这次会议的日记结尾，他写道：“生活现在将发生急剧转变。宪法不仅仅是一张废纸！这是许多人，哦，太多人都不明白的！”几周后他又写道：“哦，这是一个多么巨大的转变：真正的历史降临在我们身上，我们有幸见证这些转变，当斯大林无情地砍掉一切，所有不合格的、衰弱的、腐朽的、空虚的……生活现在已转向新的、真实的；唯有如此，我们才能走向真正的共产主义。谁说不是，谁就在撒谎！”

While decreeing a turn in his personal life, he noted in his diary that the entire Soviet system likewise stood at a crossroads. In November 1936 the Eighth Congress of Soviets ratified the new Soviet Constitution, which was officially praised as the most democratic in the world. Among other civic entitlements, the constitution foresaw a secret ballot in elections to all the state’s representative bodies, including the newly established Supreme Soviet. The first election to the Supreme Soviet was scheduled to take place in late 1937. In the months following the ratification of the constitution, the Soviet press publicized several Central Committee resolutions that called for a more democratic process in the upcoming election campaign and exhorted rank-and-file party members to be more critical of the performance of their local leaders. As Pravda reported in March and April 1937, after the introduction of secret balloting in local elections, numerous officeholders had been voted out of office. Afinogenov was impressed by the quality of self-criticism suffusing a meeting of the Moscow party organization in early 1937. In concluding his entry about this meeting he wrote: “Life will take a sharp turn now. The Constitution is not just a scrap of paper! This is what many don’t understand, oh so many!” And a few weeks later: “Oh, what a gigantic turn: genuine History is upon us, and we are granted the joy of witnessing these turns, when Stalin mercilessly chops off all and everything, all the unfit and weakened, the decaying and empty . . . Life has now taken a turn onto the new, the real; in this way and no other will we march forward to genuine Communism. Whoever says otherwise is lying!”

对阿菲诺格诺夫而言，净化党内队伍的运动是国家生活以及他个人生活中的一个关键时刻。这是涉及社会领域和个人自我的革命性净化议程的顶峰。他面临的决定性问题是，他是否足够纯洁，能够要求在社会主义世界中拥有一个正当的地位。他的日记揭示，他从一开始就深入参与了这场最终在大清洗中达到顶峰的净化运动。1937年初，在他成为恐怖目标之前，阿菲诺格诺夫将大清洗理解为他自我救赎并向所有人表明他内心是一个布尔什维克的最后机会。

For Afinogenov the campaign to purify the party’s ranks amounted to a threshold moment in the life of the country as well as his personal life. It was the culmination of a revolutionary agenda of purification involving both the social realm and individual selves. The decisive question he faced was whether he was sufficiently pure to claim a rightful place in the socialist world. His diary reveals that he was deeply involved from the start in the purification campaign that was to peak in the Great Purge. In early 1937, before he was targeted by the terror, Afinogenov understood the purge as his last chance to redeem himself and to show everybody that he was a Bolshevik at heart.
大约在同一时期，阿菲诺格诺夫的日记性质发生了变化：内省的目光变得越来越突出，几乎完全取代了日记作为作家速写本的另一个用途。阿菲诺格诺夫对灵魂状态的反思欲望增强，也体现在他更频繁地使用第一人称“我”而不是“他”来指代自己。这种转变表明了更大的心理即时性，但也表达了一种感觉，即事件发生得如此之快，以至于他没有时间和分析距离来将自己视为一个文学人物进行反思。

At about the same time, Afinogenov’s diary changed in character: the introspective gaze became ever more prominent and nearly eclipsed the diary’s other purpose as a writer’s sketchbook. Afinogenov’s increased urge to reflect on the state of his soul is also conveyed in his more frequent use of the first-person “I,” rather than “he,” to refer to himself. This switch suggests greater psychological immediacy, but it also expresses a sense that events unfolded so swiftly that he lacked time and analytical distance to reflect on himself as a literary character.
在此期间，他写日记的频率更高，条目也更长。几乎没有一天不写至少一页打字稿，而且他某一天的条目常常跨越三页或更多页。如果苏联社会成员被认为随着政权加强镇压政策而停止写日记，那么阿菲诺格诺夫的案例则指向了一种不同的动态：对他而言，恐怖激发了一场真正的自传体写作的爆发。

He wrote in his diary more often in this period, and the entries were longer. Hardly a day passed without his writing at least one typewritten page, and often his entries for a given day spanned three or more pages. If members of Soviet society are thought to have ceased keeping diaries as the regime stepped up its repressive policies, Afinogenov’s case points to a different dynamic: for him the terror induced a veritable explosion of autobiographical writing.

在这个案例中，斯大林主义的大清洗并非国家与公民之间绝对疏远的表现，而是个体与国家之间一种强烈的协同联系，其中社会净化和个体自我净化的各自议程融合在一起。阿菲诺格诺夫的日记表明，恐怖现象远不止是一种从外部威胁自我完整性的政策；它对自我产生了深刻的建构性影响，这种影响通过大量旨在净化和重塑自我的忏悔式写作表现出来。随着斯大林主义政权加大了揭露托洛茨基主义敌人的要求，阿菲诺格诺夫通过他的日记审视并净化了他的灵魂。

The Stalinist purge emerges in his case not as an expression of absolute estrangement between state and citizens, but as an intense synergetic link between individuals and the state, in which the respective agendas of social purification and individual self-purification fused. The phenomenon of terror, Afinogenov’s diary suggests, was far more than a policy threatening the integrity of the self from without; it had a profoundly constitutive effect on the self, which was expressed in torrents of confessional writing designed to cleanse and rework the self. As the Stalinist regime increased its demands for the unmasking of Trotskyist enemies, Afinogenov by means of his diary proceeded to scrutinize and cleanse his soul.

1937年3月29日和4月1日，斯大林在3月初中央委员会全会上的两篇讲话相继发表，官方的自我批评运动由此进入新阶段，他在讲话中要求揭露数千名渗透到党内的敌人。在整个苏联，这些讲话的发表引发了一场敌对分子搜捕、指控、反指控和忏悔的雪崩。正如一位大清洗的同代人后来回忆的那样，“宽敞拥挤的报告厅变成了公共忏悔室。”斯大林第一次讲话发表后仅仅几天，莫斯科剧作家协会（苏联作家联盟的一个分支）就紧急召开会议，“讨论中央委员会全会的决定。”

The official campaign of self-criticism reached a new stage with the publication, on March 29 and April 1, 1937, of two speeches Stalin had delivered to the Central Committee plenum in early March, in which he demanded the unmasking of thousands of enemies who had infiltrated the party. Throughout the Soviet Union, the publication of these speeches set off an avalanche of enemy-hunting, accusations, counter-accusations, and confessions. As a contemporary of the purge campaign later remembered, “large and crowded lecture halls were turned into public confessionals.” Within only a few days of the publication of Stalin’s first speech, a meeting of the Moscow Association of Playwrights (a division of the Soviet Writers’ Union) was hurriedly convened to “discuss the decisions of the CC plenum.”

按照中央委员会提供的指导方针，剧作家会议主要致力于揭露敌人和曝光他们协会内部的腐败官僚结构。4月4日，会议进行期间，《真理报》刊登了一则爆炸性新闻短讯：直到1936年秋天为止担任内务人民委员部（NKVD）首长的亨利希·雅戈达已被剥夺所有官方职务，并被指控犯有犯罪活动而被捕。对阿菲诺格诺夫来说，这条消息令人警觉。他与另一位剧作家弗拉基米尔·基尔雄曾与雅戈达保持密切联系，并且是雅戈达在莫斯科郊外别墅的常客。阿菲诺格诺夫与雅戈达的关系在莫斯科会议上并未被提及，但他和许多同事一起受到了批评，原因是他作为文学官员的表现以及未能进行足够的自我批评，即未能批评他剧本中的政治错误。此外，阿菲诺格诺夫在他的日记中提到，他的一些同事认为他已经被捕，还有一些人试图避开他。

In keeping with the guidelines provided by the Central Committee, the meeting of playwrights was devoted primarily to the unmasking of enemies and the exposure of corrupt bureaucratic structures within their association. On April 4, while the meeting was under way, Pravda carried a short notice containing explosive news: Genrikh Yagoda, head of the NKVD until the fall of 1936, had been stripped of all his official functions and arrested on charges of criminal activities. For Afinogenov this information was alarming. He and another playwright, Vladimir Kirshon, had been in close contact with Yagoda and had been frequent guests at Yagoda’s dacha outside Moscow. Afinogenov’s ties to Yagoda were not addressed at the Moscow meeting, but he was criticized, together with many of his colleagues, for his record as a literary official and for failing to practice sufficient self-criticism, that is, to criticize the political mistakes of his plays. Furthermore, Afinogenov noted in his diary, a number of his colleagues believed he had already been arrested, and others tried to avoid him.

两周后，事态急转直下。 《真理报》报道揭露了一个由前俄罗斯无产阶级作家协会（RAPP）秘书利奥波德·阿维尔巴赫领导的文学圈子。据说这个圈子建立了“文学中的托洛茨基主义代理机构”，并密谋破坏苏联制度。阿维尔巴赫已于4月初作为托洛茨基主义人民的敌人被捕，他娶了雅戈达的一位姐妹。除了阿维尔巴赫，《真理报》还将阿菲诺格诺夫和基尔雄认定为阴谋的领导者。在此背景下，莫斯科剧作家协会于4月27日又召开了一次会议。秘书弗谢沃洛德·维什涅夫斯基在整篇讲话中着重讨论阿维尔巴赫的罪行以及将他阵营的所有成员从协会中清除的必要性。他指控的要点是针对基尔雄的。但阿菲诺格诺夫显然是这次集会的另一个目标，他在维什涅夫斯基和基尔雄之后，被安排在第三个发言。

Events took a dramatic turn for the worse two weeks later. Pravda reported the unmasking of a literary circle led by Leopold Averbakh, the former secretary of RAPP. The circle was said to have set up a “Trotskyist agency in literature” and plotted to undermine the Soviet system. Averbakh, who had been arrested earlier in April as a Trotskyist enemy of the people, was married to Yagoda’s sister. Along with Averbakh, Pravda identified Afinogenov and Kirshon as leaders of the conspiracy. Against this background, another meeting of the Moscow Association of Playwrights was convened on April 27. The secretary, Vsevolod Vishnevsky, devoted his entire speech to Averbakh’s crimes and the need to excise all members of his camp from the association. The gist of his accusations was directed against Kirshon. But Afinogenov was evidently another target of the gathering, being third in the assigned speaking order, following Vishnevsky and Kirshon.

基尔雄坚决否认维什涅夫斯基的指控，坚称自己作为一名共产党员的精神纯洁性。和基尔雄一样，阿菲诺格诺夫首先驳斥了针对他的具体指控，即他曾与阿维尔巴赫密谋破坏苏联制度。但他随后利用这个公共场合揭露了他内心的腐败，并通过自我净化扭转了堕落的过程。他承认犯下了比他被指控的“严重得多”的错误，这些错误在他被允许发言的十五分钟内无法概括。经过一周的失眠之夜，他清楚地认识到自己是怎样一个人。通过与阿维尔巴赫和其他“文学界的名角”的接触，他“不知不觉地，一点一滴地，吸入了毫无原则的毒素，并在与他人的关系中培养了一种无知和粗野的自负和官僚主义态度，这种态度是这位文学界名角[阿维尔巴赫]所完全具备的。”这些品质“腐蚀了”阿菲诺格诺夫。在阿维尔巴赫的影响下，他背离了党，创作出“完全不是国家对我所要求和期望”的作品。“我不明白为什么我忘记了倾听国家的声音，为什么我忘记了如何写作。”他总结自己的忏悔：“作为一个人，作为一名作家和一名党员，我开始堕落。”

Kirshon emphatically denied Vishnevsky’s accusation, insisting on his spiritual purity as a Communist. Like Kirshon, Afinogenov began by refuting the specific charges against him, namely that he had been involved in a conspiracy with Averbakh to undermine the Soviet system. But he then used the public forum to expose his own inner corruption and by cleansing himself reverse the process of degeneration. He admitted to “much more serious” errors than those with which he was charged, errors impossible to summarize in the fifteen minutes he was allowed to speak. After a week of sleepless nights he had realized clearly what kind of person he was. Through his contacts with Averbakh and other “literary prima donnas,” he had “imperceptibly imbibed, drop by drop, the very poison of unprincipledness, and cultivated in my relationships with others an ignorant and boorish attitude of conceit and bureaucratism, which this literary prima donna [Averbakh] possessed in full measure.” These qualities had “corrupted” Afinogenov. Under Averbakh’s influence he had turned away from the party and produced pieces that were “absolutely not what the country demanded and wanted from me. I didn’t understand why I forgot to listen to the country and why I forgot how to write.” He summarized his confession: “As a person, as a writer and a party member, I began to degenerate.”
然而，阿菲诺格诺夫断言，他目前的处境构成了他人生中的一个转折点。对他的指控给了他一个最后的机会去“理解和认识”他过去的生活，“那是一种明显地毁灭我的生活，先是缓慢地，然后是越来越快地。”他宣称他“彻底且绝对地认识到了那种名为‘阿维尔巴赫麻风病’的毒害性疾病的本质——这是一种需要外科手术干预的疾病。”最后，他恳求他的同事们承认他已彻底与过去决裂，并在自我革新的艰难道路上迈出了第一步。

Afinogenov affirmed, however, that his current situation constituted a turning point in his life. The charges against him had given him a final opportunity to “understand and appreciate” his past life “as a life which clearly destroyed me, gradually at first, but then with increasing speed.” He declared that he had “realized, conclusively and absolutely, the essence of the poisonous disease that goes by the name of ‘Averbakh leprosy’—a disease that requires surgical intervention.” In concluding, he implored his colleagues to acknowledge that he had broken with his past once and for all and taken the first step on the difficult road of self-renewal.

聚集的剧作家们无视他的恳求。几个人承认他的忏悔是真诚的，不像基尔雄的辩护，在他们看来那简直是“狡猾律师的言辞”。然而，正是他的这份真诚，向他们表明了他与党的精神是多么格格不入。正如一位发言者所言，这种对“党的真正作用”缺乏理解，是他“过去几年戏剧创作中最严重的罪过之一”。在为期四天的会议中，三十多位作家公开抨击“托洛茨基主义者阿维尔巴赫的爪牙”基尔雄和阿菲诺格诺夫。协会通过了一项动议，讨论将他们从作家联盟理事会除名。

The assembled playwrights ignored his plea. Several conceded that his confession had been sincere, unlike Kirshon’s defense, which amounted in their eyes to a “crafty lawyer’s speech.” Yet in his very sincerity, Afinogenov had demonstrated to them just how alien he was to the spirit of the party. As one speaker remarked, this lack of understanding of “the real role of the party” was “one of the gravest sins of his dramaturgic work of the past years.” In the course of the four-day meeting, more than thirty writers spoke out against the “henchmen of the Trotskyist Averbakh,” Kirshon and Afinogenov. The association passed a motion to discuss their removal from the board of the Writers’ Union.

阿菲诺格诺夫和基尔雄都于1937年5月被开除党籍。基尔雄于1937年8月被捕，并于1938年6月被处决。阿菲诺格诺夫暂时保持自由。他被内务人民委员部从莫斯科的公寓中驱逐，搬到了他在佩列杰尔基诺作家村的别墅，与妻子、新生女儿和一名管家过着几乎完全隐居的生活。电话一连好几天悄无声息，阿菲诺格诺夫痛苦地评论那些曾经的朋友，他们都变得像兔子一样胆小。他坐在门廊上，看着作家村的邻居们走过他的别墅时故意避开视线，甚至不愿施以冷淡的问候。收音机是他与外界的主要联系：“来自遥远世界的声音、管弦乐和笑声、演讲和歌剧——他聆听一切，从而融入了他曾被排斥的世界。”那个世界似乎正在等待他的灭亡。有一天，在郊区火车上，阿菲诺格诺夫无意中听到两名军官的对话，他们对“日本间谍阿维尔巴赫”终于被处理掉，以及“阿维尔巴赫的爪牙阿菲诺格诺夫”现在已被关押等待审判表示满意。

Both Afinogenov and Kirshon were expelled from the party in May 1937. Kirshon was arrested in August 1937 and executed in June 1938. Afinogenov remained free for the time being. Evicted by the NKVD from his Moscow apartment, he moved to his dacha in the writer’s colony of Peredelkino, where he lived with his wife, their newborn daughter, and a housekeeper in nearly total seclusion. The telephone remained silent for days on end, and Afinogenov commented bitterly on former friends who had turned out to be as fearful as rabbits. Sitting on his porch, he watched as neighbors in the writers’ colony deliberately looked the other way as they walked past his dacha, unwilling to extend even a cold greeting. The radio was his principal link to the outside world: “Voices from distant worlds, orchestras and laughter, speeches and operas—he listened to everything, thereby joining the world from which he had been excluded.” That world appeared to be awaiting his annihilation. One day, on a suburban train, Afinogenov overheard a conversation between two military officers who expressed satisfaction that the “Japanese spy Averbakh” had finally been dealt with, and that “Averbakh’s henchman Afinogenov” was now in jail awaiting trial.

在等待命运的裁决并观察莫斯科和佩列杰尔基诺周围共产主义精英被捕浪潮的同时，阿菲诺格诺夫利用他的日记来思考他为何成为恐怖运动的目标，以及大清洗政策的整体动机是什么。他的个人记录与他在剧作家会议上的公开自我谴责密切呼应。会议两天后，阿菲诺格诺夫在他的日记中又写下了一份全面的忏悔，扩展了他的公开叙述。他再次承认自己的罪过，作为自我净化的一个步骤：“大净化的日子啊！针对我的言辞越是邪恶和可怕，我的精神就越是振奋。这些话一点也不可怕，人们也一点不邪恶，他们只是从自己的角度说出了真相。而且我对自己做出了更严厉的判决，因此人们的判决不再让我感到害怕。”阿菲诺格诺夫乐于接受针对他的每一项指控，因为他受到的批评越严厉，他就越能认识和谴责自己的罪恶，也就越能变得纯洁。

While waiting to learn his fate and observing the waves of arrests which engulfed the Communist elite both in Moscow and around him in Peredelkino, Afinogenov used his diary to grapple with questions of why he had become a target of the terror campaign and what motivated the purge policies as a whole. His personal record closely replicated his public self-accusation at the playwrights’ meeting. Two days after the meeting, Afinogenov produced in his diary another full-fledged confession, expanding on his public narrative. Again, he confessed his sins as a step toward self-purification: “Days of great cleansing!  The more evil and terrible the words addressed to me become, the more my spirits rise. These words aren’t terrible at all, and the people are not a bit evil, they are speaking the truth from their point of view. And I have pronounced a much harsher verdict on myself, and therefore people’s verdicts no longer frighten me.” Afinogenov relished each accusation leveled against him, for the more severely he was criticized, the more he would be able to recognize and denounce his sins and the purer he could become.

随后，他详细阐述了他在自我革新方面已经完成的工作。日记清楚地表明，在剧作家会议上的公开忏悔在这个项目中扮演了核心角色。那是一个他否定甚至扼杀了旧我的行为；是阿菲诺格诺夫所追求的“重生”的必要前提。回想起他在会议上的讲话，他曾谈到需要“外科手术干预”来清除他的阿维尔巴赫病，他现在报告说他已成功地对自己进行了一次手术，不仅切除了“胃，而且连心脏也切除了。”仅仅切除象征着他安逸富裕生活的胃是不够的；这场净化针对的是他作为一个人的本质：
我杀死了我内在的自我——然后奇迹发生了：不再抱有任何希望，并且已经为这次死亡做好了准备的我，突然理解并看到了某种全新的开始，一个新的“自我”，远离了过去的烦恼和虚荣，一个从我内心曾经拥有的、已经褪色、消失、蒸发的一切美好之中升起的“自我”。而现在它却表明它并没有褪色或蒸发，它并没有完全死去，而是为新的——即使仍然非常微弱和渺小——开始奠定了基础，在这个新的开始中，我身体的新主人对我说话。

He then detailed the work he had already performed on his self-re-newal. The diary makes clear that the public confession to the meeting of playwrights played a central role in this project. It was the act in which he had renounced, indeed killed, his former self; a necessary pre-condition for the type of “rebirth” Afinogenov aimed for. Harking back  to his speech at the meeting, where he had spoken of the need for “surgical intervention” to remove his Averbakhian disease, he now reported that he had successfully carried out an operation on himself, removing “not only the stomach, but the heart as well.” It was not enough to cut out the stomach, which symbolized his life of complacent affluence; the purge targeted his very essence as a person:

I killed the self inside me—and then a miracle happened: no longer hoping for anything and having already prepared myself for this death, I understood and suddenly saw the beginning of something altogether new, a new “self,” far removed from previous troubles and vanity, a “self” that arose out of the mist of all the best that had ever been in me and that had faded, vanished, evaporated. And now it turns out that it hasn’t faded or evaporated, it hasn’t died completely but has laid the foundation of a new—if still very weak and small—beginning, in which the new master of my body speaks to me.
