在描述他如何摆脱旧我并邀请一个新主人进入他的身体时，阿菲诺格诺夫采用了一种根本性皈依的叙事，类似于基督教的重生观念。在基督教神学中，重生是信徒达到救赎阶段的行为，他们抛弃旧的罪恶本性，在上帝的灵里获得新生命。在苏联语境中，重生经常被用来描述加入共产党的个人的内在转变。通过入党，入党者获得了新的洞察力和理解；他“重生了”，“看到了”，“知道了”，并“谈论”着新的事物，因为在那一刻他离开了世俗现实的世界，进入了一个更高知识和愿景的领域。

重生概念对于阿菲诺格诺夫在大清洗背景下的主体性至关重要，因为它允许他包容他过去的罪恶，同时又给了他最终得救的保证。由于重生预设了先前有罪的自我的存在，阿菲诺格诺夫可以将这个自我识别为“堕落的剧作家阿菲诺格诺夫”，正如他的指控者给他贴上的标签，也是他自己对自己的看法。然而，同样地，他能够通过忏悔的行为来否定这个自我。通过在重生前经历一次象征性的死亡，他可以声称自己已作为一个全新的、纯洁的生命而出现，与过去的阿菲诺格诺夫不再有任何共同之处。他在日记中提到，报纸上对他的攻击是针对一个“因误解而被称为我名字的死尸”的。

In describing how he shed his former self and invited a new master into his body, Afinogenov employed a narrative of radical conversion akin to the Christian notion of rebirth. Rebirth in Christian theology is the act by which the believer reaches the stage of salvation, leaving behind his old sinful nature and attaining a new life in God’s spirit. In the Soviet context, rebirth was frequently used to describe the inner transformation of a person who joined the Communist party. By joining the party, the initiate reached new insight and understanding; he was “born anew,” “saw,” “knew,” and “spoke of” new things, for in that moment he left the world of profane reality and entered a realm of higher knowledge and vision.

The notion of rebirth was essential to Afinogenov’s subjectivity in the context of the purges, for it allowed him to accommodate his past sins while at the same time giving him the assurance that he would eventually be saved. Since rebirth presupposes the existence of a prior, sinful self, Afinogenov could identify this self as the “degenerate playwright Afinogenov,” as he had been labeled by his accusers but as he also saw himself. By the same token, however, he was able to re-nounce this self through the act of confession. By undergoing a symbolic death prior to being reborn, he could claim that he had emerged as a new, pure being who no longer had anything in common with the old Afinogenov. In his diary he remarked that the attacks against him in the newspapers were being directed against a “dead body which by a misunderstanding is called by my name.”

即使在摆脱旧我并作为新人重生之后，阿菲诺格诺夫仍不得不面对对其自我革新主张可信度的问题。他的批评者拒绝了他主张所依据的前提，即他曾是一名堕落的党员，一个暂时失去清醒意识但现在已坚定重回正轨的犯错布尔什维克。正如《文学报》在他被开除党籍时所评论的那样：“阿菲诺格诺夫的所有活动……表明他之所以不能被称为一个堕落的[党员]，唯一的原因是他一直是一个从根本上与党格格不入的人。”仿佛是为了回应这个毁灭性的判决，阿菲诺格诺夫在他的日记中纲领性地写道：“这个新我是这样一个人：总有一天人民会听到他的声音，他们会明白，这个声音就是一个布尔什维克的声音，无论如何！”鉴于阿菲诺格诺夫被排除在集体之外，日记几乎是他决心成为的布尔什维克可以发出和训练自己声音的唯一媒介。

Even after having shed his former self and been reborn as a new person, Afinogenov had to face questions about the credibility of his claim to self-renewal. His critics rejected the very premise on which he had based his claim, namely, that he had been a degenerate party member, an erring Bolshevik who had temporarily slid from full consciousness but was now firmly back on track. As Literaturnaya gazeta remarked on the occasion of his expulsion from the party: “All of Afinogenov’s activities . . . show that the only reason he can’t be called a degenerate [party member] is that he has always been a person who was fundamentally alien to the party.” As if in response to this damning verdict, Afinogenov stated programmatically in his diary: “This new self is a person whose word the people will hear at some point, and they will understand that this word is the word of a Bolshevik, no matter what!” Given Afinogenov’s exclusion from the collective, the diary was practically the only medium in which the Bolshevik he was determined to become could raise and train his voice.

然而，将阿菲诺格诺夫1937年的日记简化为一份布尔什维克式的自我塑造叙述将是误导性的。相反，这本日记以多种声音说话。它描绘了一个被集体排斥的个体，绝望地试图理解他个人存在与席卷他的政治进程之间的关系。期待与怀疑、希望与痛苦迅速交织。就在他忏悔和自我革新几天后，阿菲诺格诺夫在日记中对自己的描述截然不同，他坚称自己是无辜的，并怀疑对他的谴责是“恶魔般的”法西斯阴谋的一部分，旨在“消灭有才华的苏联艺术家”。他白天似乎获得的清醒头脑，与黑暗时分的绝望时刻交替出现：“傍晚降临，一股新的沮丧和痛苦爆发……为什么？为什么？……贝拉·伊列什服毒了。我仍然更坚强，但谁知道呢，也许我很快就会精疲力尽，发出响亮的声明，用一个不属于我的声音，说出一些绝对可怕的事情！人们在哪里？支持和安慰的声音在哪里？救赎和生命在哪里？”

It would be misleading, however, to reduce Afinogenov’s diary of 1937 to a narrative of self-fashioning in a Bolshevik vein. Rather, the diary speaks in several voices. It portrays an individual excluded from the collective, desperately trying to make sense of his personal existence in relationship to the political process engulfing him. In rapid succession, expectations are paired with doubts, hope with anguish. Only days after his confession and self-renewal, Afinogenov spoke of himself very differently in his diary, maintaining that he was innocent and suspecting that his denunciation was part of a “devilish” fascist conspiracy seeking to “annihilate talented Soviet artists.” The clarity of mind that he seemed to attain during the day oscillated with moments of despair in the darker hours: “The evening sets in, and a renewed outburst of depression and pain . . . What for? What for? . . . Bela Illesh has poisoned himself. I’m still sturdier, but who knows, maybe I will soon run out of strength and make loud statements, with a voice that is not mine, about something absolutely horrible! Where are the people? Where is the voice of support and comfort? Where is salvation and life?”

类似的摇摆不定也体现在阿菲诺格诺夫对1937年5月20日被共产党开除的官方决定的反应上。他当日的日记描述了作家联盟党支部会议，会上党书记亚历山大·法捷耶夫“面无表情地称我为粗俗而平庸的人，一个堕落的资产阶级，一个一无是处的艺术家。”随后，所有支部成员公开投票将他开除党籍。当会议转向议程的另一个议题时，阿菲诺格诺夫起身，在“死寂”中离开了房间。他一走出房间，就恢复了“平静，几乎是快乐”，因为他知道自己“没有任何罪过”。然而，当天晚些时候，当同事伊利亚·塞尔文斯基来家中“安慰并鼓励他”时，他的心情又有所不同：
我们谈到了一个人的整个人生，其中不可能没有错误。然后，当你必须为某个错误负责时，突然之间，所有人都忘记了这个人一生中可能做过、并且很可能做过的所有好事。就像格蕾琴一样，她一生都过着贞洁、纯洁、无罪、善良的生活。但她只与浮士德犯了一次罪，就这一次，她便抛下过去所有的虔诚和善良，从天堂之门直接坠入地狱。

Similar vacillation characterized Afinogenov’s reactions to the official decision to expel him from the Communist party on May 20, 1937. His entry of that day described the meeting of the party section of the Writers’ Union during which party secretary Alexander Fadeev “with a stony face called me a vulgar and philistine person, a degenerate bourgeois, and a good-for-nothing artist.” All members of the section then openly voted to expel him from the party. When the meeting turned to a different point on the agenda, Afinogenov got up and left the room “in deadly silence.” As soon as he was outside, he regained his “calm, bordering on happiness,” because he knew that he was “not guilty of anything.” His mood was different later in the day, however, when a colleague, Ilya Selvinsky, visited him at home to “comfort him and cheer him up”:

We spoke about the entire life of a person, in which there cannot not be any mistakes. And then when you have to answer for a mistake, all of a sudden everybody forgets about all the good things that this person could have done in his life and which he probably had done. Like Gretchen, who lived her entire life in a chaste and pure, sinless and good way. But she had only to commit one sin, just one, with Faust, for all her previous piety and goodness, to go from the gates of heaven straight to hell.

阿菲诺格诺夫将自己比作格蕾琴，承认自己对党犯了罪，尽管他与塞尔文斯基的谈话也表明他认为自己的惩罚过于严厉。阿菲诺格诺夫被开除党籍，这代表了他罪恶自我的公开曝光，因此即使在私人对话等非官方场合，也迫使他接受自己的堕落。此外，他将这次谈话记录在日记中，从而给自己刚刚宣称的无罪附加了限制。正如他进一步指出的那样，在被开除党籍后的几天和几周里，他研究了失宠、牺牲和救赎的概念。他在塞万提斯、布鲁诺·弗兰克和陀思妥耶夫斯基的作品中，希望能找到精神指导的模式：“是的，现在，在孤独中，他终于感到了渴望去理解以前未曾完成的事情。他想阅读关于人生哲学的作品，不是为了某种‘教育’，而是因为他需要一个即时的答案，关于今后如何与人相处，如何对待他们，以及如何为人处世。”

Likening himself to Gretchen, Afinogenov admitted to having sinned against the party, even if his discussion with Selvinsky also suggests that he believed his punishment to have been unduly harsh. Afinogenov’s expulsion from the party, which stood for the public exposure of his sinful self, thus compelled him to accept his depravity even in a non-official setting such as a private conversation. Moreover, he recorded this conversation in his diary, thereby qualifying the proclamation of innocence he had just made. As he further noted, he spent the days and weeks following his expulsion researching the concepts of fall from grace, sacrifice, and redemption. In works by Cervantes, Bruno Frank, and Dostoevsky, he hoped to find models of spiritual guidance: “Yes, now, in solitude, he felt at last the urge to comprehend that which earlier had not been accomplished. He wanted to read works on the philosophy of life not for the sake of some kind of ‘education,’ but because he needed an immediate answer to the questions of how to live henceforth with people, how to relate to them, and how to conduct himself.”

为了成为一个新的人，阿菲诺格诺夫决定对自己的生活做出彻底的改变。摆脱他过去堕落的自我，首先意味着结束他那种茫然无知、追求享乐的生活方式。但这也意味着抛弃那些曾腐蚀过他的老朋友和同事。阿菲诺格诺夫曾在日记中写道，他过去的大多数伙伴都变成了“敌人”：他们“要么被捕，要么被批得体无完肤”。由于怀疑更多熟人很快会作为人民的敌人被捕，阿菲诺格诺夫在自我净化的道路上走得更远。在他看来，逮捕最频繁的整个莫斯科市都变成了污染之地。他决定避开这个危险的污染源，转而追求在佩列杰尔基诺的孤立生活：“总的来说，每次去莫斯科都是一次神经震撼。你不能再去那里了，你必须独自生活，你必须休息，并为自己还活着而感到高兴，可以躺在阳光下，除了你那微小而简单的生活之外，什么都不想，只有你了解这种生活。”

In his attempt to become a new person, Afinogenov resolved to make drastic changes in his life. Shedding his former corrupted self entailed first and foremost an end to his oblivious and pleasure-seeking way of life. But it also meant leaving behind former friends and colleagues, exposure to whom had corrupted him. Afinogenov once observed in his diary that most of his former associates had turned out to be “enemies”: they had been “either arrested or picked to pieces.” Suspecting that many more acquaintances would soon be arrested as enemies of the people, Afinogenov went even further in search of self-purification. In his eyes the entire city of Moscow, where arrests were most frequent, became a site of pollution. He resolved to avoid this dangerous source of contamination and to pursue instead an isolated existence in Peredelkino: “On the whole, every trip to Moscow is a nervous shock. You mustn’t go there anymore, you must live alone by yourself, you must rest and be glad that you are alive and can lie in the sun without thinking about anything except your small and simple life, which alone you understand.”
阿菲诺格诺夫含蓄地将纯洁的“微小而简单的生活，只有你了解”与一个道德败坏、充满隐匿敌人并蓄意背叛的险恶世界并置。他梦想着抛弃自己不纯洁的社会环境，寻求在一个偏远地方避难：
成为一个隐士，独自一人或与我的孩子一起安顿下来——不依赖任何人，不受任何人的束缚。我现在害怕人群，尽管我偶尔会有一种和他们坐在一起聊天的冲动，但我还是害怕。这是一次如此深刻的人生教训，那些你最信任的人结果却成了叛徒和敌人。现在，除了我自己，我不信任任何人。我不能为任何人担保，我想远远地离开，以一种不与任何人接触的方式生活。

Afinogenov implicitly juxtaposed the pure, “small and simple life, which alone you understand” to a morally depraved, treacherous world filled with hidden enemies intent on betrayal. He dreamed of leaving behind his impure social environment and seeking refuge in a remote place:

Become a hermit, settle either alone or with my child—and not depend on anybody, not be tied down by anybody. I’m afraid of people now, although I have this occasional urge to sit with them and talk, but I’m afraid. This was such a life lesson, when the people you trusted most of all turned out to be traitors and enemies. Now, except myself, I don’t trust anybody. I can’t vouch for anybody and I want to go far away and live in such a way that I don’t have contact with anybody.
像鲁滨逊·克鲁索一样生活在自我流放中，并在逮捕浪潮持续不断——这些逮捕也给作家村的居民造成了损失——的背景下，阿菲诺格诺夫开始推崇与布尔什维克关于人是集体存在的观念完全背道而驰的价值观。阿菲诺格诺夫不仅发现了一种私人化的“为自己而活”的生活——这对于一个忠诚的共产党员来说是一个禁忌——是可行的；他将其描述为一种最高形式的自我实现：
他们打牌，他手气很好。然后他们喝茶，吃了樱桃馅的甜饺子。他回家了，那是一个温暖的夏夜。在星空下漫步，他吹着口哨，温柔地感谢生活，感谢现在对他来说如此清晰和宁静。他突然明白，他一直都想要这样一种平静的生活，即使代价是如此可怕的灾难。那都没关系。现在，没有人需要他了，让他高兴的是他可以为自己而活。

Living like Robinson Crusoe in his self-imposed exile, and in the midst of continuous waves of arrests, which were also taking their toll among residents of the writers’ colony, Afinogenov came to extol values wholly at odds with the Bolshevik notion of man as a collective being. Afinogenov not only discovered that a private “life for himself”—anathema for a dedicated Communist—was viable; he described it as a highest form of self-realization:

They played cards, he had a streak of luck. Then they drank tea and ate sweet pierogi with cherry filling. He went home, it was a warm summer night. Strolling under the stars, he whistled and tenderly thanked life that it was now so clear and peaceful for him. He suddenly understood that he had always wanted a peaceful life like this, even at the price of such a terrible catastrophe. It didn’t matter. Now he was not needed by anybody and what made him happy was that he could live for himself.
从接受独居生活的新理想到谴责他过去为党服务的生活，只是一小步：

奇怪的事情发生在我身上。从14岁起我就不再属于自己。先是共青团，然后是党。我一直肩负着某种牺牲的意识。我是一名士兵，诚实地在队伍中服役，党命令我做的每一件事我都做了，从未对此有过任何坏念头……但现在他们突然开始怀疑什么，并可耻地把我从队伍中开除了。就好像他们挖掉了我的眼睛说：我们现在不需要你了，爱去哪儿去哪儿。起初，啊，那些日子是多么可怕的孤立和孤独……好吧，我不得不离开队伍。我拿起我的包离开了。然后，当我离开城镇，随心所欲地走着的时候，我才发现，自从遥远的童年以来，自由漫步的快乐。没有人需要你，是的，没有人需要你，你想去哪儿就去哪儿，为人民和国家工作，但要独自一人，不引人注目，因为没有人需要你。没有人催你去开会，或者命令你写文章或发表演讲说些无聊的话，这真是太棒了……哦，多好啊——去你认为必要的地方工作。
It was only a small step from embracing the new ideal of a solitary life to condemning his former life in the service of the party:

Strange things are happening to me. Since the age of 14 I haven’t belonged to myself. First the Komsomol, then the party. I have always carried the consciousness of some sort of sacrifice on my shoulders. I was a soldier and honestly served in the ranks, I did everything that the party ordered me to do and had never had any bad thoughts about it . . . But now they suddenly begin to suspect something and have ignominiously removed me from the ranks. It is as if they had cut out my eye and said: We don’t need you now, go where you want. And at first, ah, what terrible days of isolation and solitude these were . . . Oh well, I had to leave the ranks. I took my bag and left. And then, as I was leaving town and following my nose, I discovered for the first time since my distant childhood the happiness of a free step. You are not needed by anybody, yes, nobody needs you, go where you want and work for the benefit of the people and the country, but by yourself and inconspicuously, for you are not needed. How wonderful this is that nobody is pursuing you with calls to meetings, or with orders to write an article or to give a speech and say something boring . . . Oh, how wonderful—to go and work where you deem necessary.

阿菲诺格诺夫不再将自己被开除党籍视为一种绝对的损失或失宠。相反，他将自己过去的生活描述为一种自我牺牲的行为。现在他不再是队伍中的士兵，不再执行党的命令，他发现了一种新的自由感和目标感：一种虽小但平静而稳定的存在。他被开除党籍就像他的眼睛被毁坏一样：这意味着他作为一名共产党员和一名作家曾拥有的卓越洞察力的丧失。这种洞察力曾赋予他作为人类灵魂工程师的特殊社会责任，而正是这种责任负担的丧失，让阿菲诺格诺夫在赞扬他作为“不被任何人需要”的人的新生活时心中所想。

Afinogenov no longer viewed his expulsion from the party in terms of an absolute loss or a fall from grace. On the contrary, he described his former life as an act of self-sacrifice. Now that he was no longer a soldier in the ranks, executing party orders, he discovered a new sense of freedom and purpose: a small but peaceful and stable existence. His expulsion from the party was like a mutilation of his eye: it entailed a loss of the superior vision he had previously possessed as a Communist and a writer. This vision had imposed on him particular social responsibilities as an engineer of human souls, and it was precisely the loss of this burden of responsibility that Afinogenov had in mind when hailing his new existence as someone who was “not needed by anybody.”

然而，正如阿菲诺格诺夫迫切地拥抱个人存在的理想一样，他在几周内就开始否定它。他1937年7月和8月的日记中充满了欢呼他进入意识新阶段的篇章。这些记录中的第一条写于他梦想成为隐士仅三天之后，开头写道：“这一章可以命名为‘回归生活’……在这一天，我突然感觉到生活在我周围忙碌……报纸上的文字再次唤醒了我以前的态度。”阿菲诺格诺夫继续写道：“这种亲近生活的感觉让你充满喜悦，你再次倾听‘最新消息’中的词句，你阅读关于丰收的记录，关于契卡洛夫团队的飞行以及克里姆林宫对他们的接见，所有这些都让你感到快乐和兴奋。你再次从昏睡中醒来。击昏状态结束了，人开始生活了。”

Just as urgently as Afinogenov embraced the ideal of an individual existence, however, he began to repudiate it within a few weeks. His diary of July and August 1937 is filled with passages hailing his arrival at a new stage of consciousness. The first of these entries, written only three days after his dream of becoming a hermit, began: “This chapter might be entitled ‘The Return to Life’ . . . This is a day on which I suddenly felt that life is bustling around me . . . Once again the lines of the newspapers are bringing to life my former attitude.” Afinogenov continued: “This feeling of being close to life fills you with joy, you listen once again to the words of the ‘Latest News,’ you read about the record harvest, about the flight of the Chkalov team and the reception for them in the Kremlin, and all this makes you happy and excited. And once again you awake from a lethargic sleep. The knockout is over, and the person begins to live.”
阿菲诺格诺夫现在将他早先关于自主生活的梦想称为“昏睡”时刻，称为“被击倒”阶段，暗示他在记录那些想法时缺乏任何意识。相比之下，“回归生活”包含了重新融入苏联体制，并重新参与到集体的英雄生活和历史进程中。只要他的个人存在脱离苏联人民的集体，它就是渺小且微不足道的。只有使自己与苏联体制保持一致，他才能实现自我。

几天后，他描述了一个类似的转折点，称之为“觉醒”。正如他现在透露的，在过去的几个晚上里，他一直在等待被捕。但现在他知道他的恐惧是毫无根据的：“在卢比扬卡那边，人们是睿智的。尽管他们日程繁忙，工作量惊人，但他们能洞察一切的根源……没有任何风浪会强迫他们逮捕一个无辜的人。”第二天，阿菲诺格诺夫再次庆祝他“根本性的、不同寻常的突破”，即他新获得的不会被捕的确定感。他为自己在日记中倾诉早先的恐惧而感到尴尬。为了强调他现在的感受是多么不同，他甚至质疑那些绝望念头的作者身份：“这些念头是从哪里冒出来的？是谁写的？”

Afinogenov now referred to his earlier dreams of an autonomous life as moments of “lethargic sleep,” as a “knockout” phase, implying that he had lacked any consciousness when recording those thoughts. By contrast, the “return to life” subsumed his reintegration into the Soviet system and his renewed participation in the heroic life of the collective and in the course of history. As long as his personal existence evolved away from the collective body of the Soviet people, it remained small and insignificant. Only in aligning himself with the Soviet system could he realize himself as a person.

He described a similar turning point a few days later, referring to it as an “awakening.” As he now disclosed, he had spent the past nights waiting to be arrested. But now he knew that his fears were unfounded: “Over there, at the Lubianka, the people are intelligent. Despite their busy schedules and the insane amount of work, they see down to the roots of everything . . . and no wave will force them to arrest an innocent person.” The following day Afinogenov once more celebrated his “fundamental and unusual break,” namely, his newfound certainty that he would not be arrested. He felt embarrassed that he had confided his earlier fears to the diary. To underscore how different he now felt, he even questioned the authorship of those despairing thoughts: “Where did these thoughts spring from? Who wrote them?”

阿菲诺格诺夫似乎在暗示，他体内仿佛住着两个不同的人，他们以截然相反的方式评估政治局势，因此也追求着截然不同的自我实现手段。一个生活在对被捕的永久恐惧中，梦想着一种孤独的生存，以躲避腐败的社会环境。另一个则否认被捕的可能性，甚至否认社会秩序的不纯洁，呼吁个人融入苏联体制。将这些关于个人自主和社会自我融合的分歧观念视为阿菲诺格诺夫私人自我和公共自我的表达是很诱人的——即阿菲诺格诺夫私下渴望个人独立和自由，而在公开场合维持一个符合苏联官方规范的形象。这种截然不同的身份在阿菲诺格诺夫的私人日记中上演，这一事实似乎表明他的官方自我形象在多大程度上干扰了他的自我定义，以及他要保留一种区别于政权所规定的社会身份的私人自我意识是多么困难。
然而，这种强调私人和官方自我定义之间的差异，并从私人领域优先的信念出发的解读，掩盖了阿菲诺格诺夫对自我的分歧评估之间的联系。如果我们不再孤立地对待单条记录，而是将其视为更大叙事结构中的元素，那么这本日记就呈现为一种精神写作的形式，其组织方式旨在演练“皈依”的体验。阿菲诺格诺夫将这种皈依描述为回归生活、新生，以及获得更高的意识和纯洁性。因此，日记成为了促进他个人救赎的一种手段。

Afinogenov seemed to be implying that there were two different persons living inside him, who assessed the political situation in opposite terms and therefore also pursued contrasting means of self-realization. One lived in permanent fear of arrest and dreamed of a solitary existence which would shelter him from the corrupt social environment. The other disclaimed the likelihood of arrest and, indeed, the impurity of the social order, calling for the individual’s integration into the Soviet system. It would be tempting to view these diverging notions of individual autonomy and social self-integration as expressions of Afinogenov’s private and public selves, with Afinogenov privately yearning for personal independence and freedom, while maintaining in public an image of himself that would conform to official Soviet norms. The fact that these contrasting identities were played out in Afinogenov’s private diary would seem to suggest how much his official self-image interfered with his own self-definition and how difficult it was for him to retain a private sense of himself in distinction from the social identity prescribed by the regime.

Yet this interpretation, which emphasizes the disparity between private and official self-definitions and proceeds from a belief in the primacy of the private domain, obscures the links between Afinogenov’s diverging assessments of himself. If we stop treating individual entries in isolation, and view them instead as elements of a larger narrative structure, the diary emerges as a form of spiritual writing, organized in such a way as to enact the experience of conversion. Afinogenov described this conversion variously as a return to life, a new birth, and the attainment of a higher consciousness and purity. The diary thus served as a means of furthering his personal salvation.
皈依是一个共产党员的基础体验。如果不能证明自己经历了皈依，共产党员就无法对党籍提出可信的主张。尽管形式各异，苏联早期作为入党申请程序一部分而撰写的共产主义自传，都描述了一种皈依体验，将申请人的生活分为两个阶段：早期阶段以落后、被动和缺乏意识为特征；而成熟、积极且自觉的阶段则是由接触共产党的教导而引发的。正是凭借共产党员对党的历史作用的洞察以及随后的皈依，他才获得了作为进步人类领导者的先锋地位。

阿菲诺格诺夫意识到，皈依不能简化为单一的新生体验，就像他在莫斯科剧作家会议上做完自我批评发言后所描述的那样。正如对基督徒而言，他的皈依更像是一个终身的过程，需要不断地重演和重申。最初看到光明并改过自新的时刻，无论多么富有戏剧性，都只是漫长精神生活的序曲。正如一位研究基督教皈依的学者所写，在“最初惊人的觉醒”之后，皈依者必须“始终警惕得救的恩典与再度堕落的迹象，总是质疑前者的真实性并恐惧虚假的安全感……确信感，就像喜悦、悲伤或疲劳一样，会产生其自身的另一套危险，如骄傲、绝望或自满。因此，每一项成就都可能引发新一轮的负罪感和自我测试。”

Conversion was the founding experience for a Communist. Communists could make no credible claim to party membership without proving that they had experienced conversion. For all their variations, Communist autobiographies from the early Soviet period, which were written as part of the application process for party membership, described a conversion experience dividing the lives of candidates into two phases: an early phase marked by backwardness, passivity, and a lack of consciousness; and a mature, active, and conscious phase induced by exposure to the teachings of the Communist party. It was on the strength of a Communist’s insight into the historical role of the party and his ensuing conversion that he acquired his vanguard status as a leader of progressive mankind.

Afinogenov realized that conversion could not be reduced to a single experience of rebirth, such as the one he had described after his self-critical speech at the meeting of Moscow playwrights. As with a Christian believer, his conversion was rather a lifelong process, to be reenacted and reaffirmed time and again. The initial occasion of seeing the light and turning in one’s tracks, however dramatic, constituted only a prelude to an extended spiritual life. As a scholar of Christian conversion has written, after the “initial startled awakening,” the convert had to remain “steadily alert to signs of saving grace and backsliding, always questioning the genuineness of the former and fearing false security . . . Assurance, like joy, grief, or fatigue, generates its own other set of dangers such as pride, despair, or complacency. Each achievement can thus spark another cycle of guilt and self-testing.”

在被开除出党后的这段时间里，阿菲诺格诺夫通过他的日记写作不断尝试改过自新，以达到一种更纯粹的意识形式，他有时称之为理解的“第二阶段”。例如，在听说包括以前的朋友、作家弗谢沃洛德·伊万诺夫在内的几位同事正在散布他被捕的谣言时，阿菲诺格诺夫写道：“怎么能生活在这些两面派、懦夫和胆小鬼中间呢！”然而，第二天，他采取了不同的立场：“昨天我完全没能达到第二阶段……今天我做到了，为此我感到高兴。”他写道，现在他理解了伊万诺夫行为背后那太过人性的动机；他不再愤慨，而是以理解和同情来应对。日记还记录了阿菲诺格诺夫无法维持皈依而退回到旧自我的时刻。1937年10月2日，他记下了对斯大林演讲的热情，在那次演讲中，斯大林宣布敌人往往是那些表现出过度狂热的人。形成鲜明对比的是，次日的记录充满了绝望：“忧郁，多么沉重的忧郁！……既然我已经从自信中退缩并跌回到普通状态，我突然害怕自己会撑不下去，我又开始害怕自己可能会疯掉。”几周后，再次注意到自己不断回到惯常的怀疑和恐惧中时，他责备自己：“你为什么变得软弱了？”

In the period following his expulsion from the party, Afinogenov through his diary writings consistently tried to turn in his tracks and reach a purer form of consciousness, which he sometimes referred to as a “second stage” of comprehension. For example, on hearing that a number of colleagues, among them a former friend, the writer Vsevolod Ivanov, were spreading a rumor that he was under arrest, Afinogenov wrote: “How can one live among such double-dealers, cowards and fainthearted types!” The next day, however, he took a different stance: “Yesterday I didn’t succeed at all in reaching the second stage . . . Today I did, and I’m happy about it.” Now, he wrote, he understood the all too human motivations of Ivanov’s behavior; no longer indignant, he reacted with understanding and compassion. The diary also recorded instances when Afinogenov was unable to sustain a conversion and reverted to his old self. On October 2, 1937, he noted his enthusiasm for a speech in which Stalin had declared that enemies were frequently those who showed excessive zeal. In striking contrast, the entry of the following day resounded with despair: “Depression, what leaden depression! . . . Now that I’ve retreated from my confidence and fallen back into my ordinary state, I’m suddenly afraid that I won’t be able to hold out, again I began to fear that I might lose my mind.” A few weeks later, again noting that he kept returning to his customary doubts and fears, he reprimanded himself: “Why did you become weak?”

这种确定感和自信让位于怀疑，而怀疑又以更高意识的名义被消除的辩证模式，不仅可以在日记条目的序列中观察到，在单条条目内部也能观察到。他被开除出党期间的许多记录都以怀疑、绝望和无法理解自己处境的抱怨开始。通常这些记录以自信和乐观的语调结束，阿菲诺格诺夫欢呼他重新发现的归属感和目标感。日记的功能是驱散怀疑和不和谐，以便让他达到更高形式的意识和统一。阿菲诺格诺夫将一种新“洞察力”的出现比作“几乎神秘的奇迹，通过它我获得了新生”。
事实上，从肃反运动开始，一种皈依的主旨就构成了阿菲诺格诺夫日记的整个结构。这是一个逐渐走向光明的叙事，这种进程在起初是痛苦且伴随着频繁倒退的，但后来变得越来越稳健和坚定。1937年5月，在他被开除的那天，阿菲诺格诺夫在日记中倾诉说，他无法理解这一举动。他不再是历史展开的积极参与者，他感到被一种外部力量粗暴地推搡着，因此对自己的命运感到不确定。
然而，在那年夏末，他回首失去党籍后的几个月，将其视为“击昏”阶段，一段充满了怀疑、恐惧和逃避现实梦想的时光。尽管他谴责这一阶段，但它起到了重要的作用：如果没有先前的堕落和死亡，皈依和重生的叙事就无法运作。正因如此，作为一段退步和思想软弱的时期，阿菲诺格诺夫将他的怀疑和对党的政策的初步批评融入了他日记的整体皈依叙事中。

This dialectical pattern of certainty and self-assurance giving way to doubts which in turn are dispelled in the name of a higher consciousness can be observed not only in the sequence of diary entries but within single entries as well. Many entries of the period of his exclusion from the party begin with doubts, despair, and complaints that he cannot comprehend his position. Typically these entries end on a confident and optimistic note, with Afinogenov hailing his rediscovered sense of belonging and purpose. The function of the diary was to dispel doubts and dissonance so as to allow him to achieve a higher form of consciousness and unity. Afinogenov likened the emergence of a new “insight” to an “almost mystical miracle through which I was reborn.”

In fact, a conversion motif underlies the entire structure of Afinogenov’s diary from the onset of the purge campaign. It is a narrative of a gradual coming to the light, a progression that at the outset is tortuous and marked by frequent backslidings, but that becomes increasingly steady and determined. In May 1937, on the day of his expulsion, Afinogenov confided to his diary that he could make little sense of this act. No longer an active participant in the unfolding of history, he felt brutally pushed about by an external force and therefore uncertain about his fate.

In late summer of that year, though, he looked back on months following his loss of party membership as a “knockout” phase, a time filled with doubts, fears, and escapist dreams. As much as he condemned this phase, it had served an important purpose: the narrative of conversion and rebirth could not function without a previous degeneration and death. It was as such, as a period of backsliding and weakness of mind, that Afinogenov integrated his doubts and his incipient criticism of party policies into the overall conversion narrative of his diary.

从1937年夏末开始，阿菲诺格诺夫表现出越来越深信自己已对周围运作的政治进程获得了深刻的洞察。他比以前更清楚地理解，肃反政策正为通往共产主义天堂铺平道路，个人反对这一世界历史进程是荒谬的。有了这种洞察力，阿菲诺格诺夫也认为自己有理由收回作为主要共产主义剧作家的地位，因为他现在已经达到了那种对处于革命发展中的现实的更深层理解，而这对于一名苏联艺术家来说是至关重要的。他以前缺乏这种愿景，正是过去几年所有针对他的攻击和批评的核心所在。他现在否定了他偶尔产生的放弃写作职业、成为苏联集体中一名普通成员（比如在外省某地当一名拖拉机手）的幻想。
阿菲诺格诺夫谴责了那种十九世纪后期俄罗斯知识分子典型的“小事”伦理，转而支持他现在认为的、作为一名服务于共产主义政权的苏联作家所承担的无限更有意义、能改变人生的使命。以他作为人类灵魂工程师的身份，他将拥有独特的机会，直接为创造“新人”做出贡献。

Beginning in the late summer of 1937, Afinogenov showed himself increasingly convinced that he had gained profound insight into the political processes at work around him. He understood better than before that the purge policies paved the way toward the Communist paradise and that it was ludicrous for an individual to oppose this world-historical process. With this insight, Afinogenov also saw himself as justified in reclaiming his position as a leading Communist dramatist, for he had now attained precisely the type of deeper understanding of reality in its revolutionary development that was essential to a Soviet artist. His previous lack of this vision had been at the core of all attacks and criticism against him in previous years. He now repudiated his occasional fantasy of leaving the writing profession and becoming a simple member of the Soviet collective, a tractor driver somewhere in the provinces.

Afinogenov condemned what may be termed a “small deeds” ethos typical of the late nineteenth-century Russian intelligentsia in favor of what he now considered an infinitely more meaningful, life-transforming mission as a Soviet writer serving the Communist regime. In his capacity as an engineer of human souls, he would have unique opportunities to contribute directly to the creation of the new man.

en: Inkwell on the Master’s Desk

children: 阿菲诺格诺夫是在生存处境极度不确定的背景下编写这些皈依方案的。他关于重新融入苏联宇宙的宣言，与他在社会中如同贱民般的地位相矛盾。1937年9月1日，当作家协会主席团将他从协会队伍中开除时，他的境遇进一步恶化。这是一个令人心碎的事件，一次不亚于被开除出党、甚至可能更糟的公开排斥，因为他现在失去了与苏联社会的所有制度联系，甚至不再被承认为一名作家。

Afinogenov scripted these conversion scenarios against a background of intense existential uncertainty. His proclamations of reintegration into the Soviet universe were belied by his pariah-like standing in society. His position worsened on September 1, 1937, when the presidium of the Writers’ Union expelled him from the union’s ranks. It was a shattering event, a public ostracism on a par with his expulsion from the party, or perhaps even worse, because he had now lost all institutional connection with Soviet society and was not even recognized as a writer.
他完全有理由将自己被逐出作家协会视为被捕的前奏。

在这个极度艰难的时期，极少数支持阿菲诺格诺夫的人之一是鲍里斯·帕斯捷尔纳克。这两位作家自1936年起就相识，当时他们在佩列杰尔基诺被分配到了相邻的别墅。1937年夏秋，当时帕斯捷尔纳克正在创作后来扩充为小说《日瓦戈医生》的草稿，他不怕与这位被排斥的剧作家交谈，不怕陪他在村子里长距离散步，也不怕去他的别墅探望他。他们的交谈让阿菲诺格诺夫能与一位信任的人分享他的绝望和恐惧，这个人安慰了他并帮助他保持神志清醒。除了提供这种至关重要的支持外，帕斯捷尔纳克还体现了一种令阿菲诺格诺夫着迷的个人风范。他钦佩帕斯捷尔纳克那让他对世界视而不见的文学激情：莫斯科文坛的嘈杂、作家协会的勾心斗角、媒体歌颂的英雄苏联公民的壮举。帕斯捷尔纳克的无畏尤其给阿菲诺格诺夫留下了深刻印象，这种态度根植于他的自我主宰。他是“这种充满活力的斯多葛主义的活生生榜样”。在像帕斯捷尔纳克这样的人面前，“你学到了最重要的一点——在任何情况下都能独立生活的能力。”但是，虽然他钦佩帕斯捷尔纳克那“水晶般的透明”和对他艺术的专注奉献，阿菲诺格诺夫却不能也不愿为自己采纳这种行为模式。帕斯捷尔纳克不看报纸、不听广播，这让他感到惊讶：“这对我来说太奇怪了，我一天不看新闻都活不下去。”对阿菲诺格诺夫来说，居住在世界上是绝对必要的，而不是以一种斯多葛式的冷漠姿态置身于世界之外。这个世界就是新兴社会主义社会的宇宙。即使那个社会禁止他被承认为文化领袖，他也禁不住要关注它的建设，因为它通过报纸的字里行间和广播的声音传递出来。
He had every reason to see his removal from the Writers’ Union as a prelude to his arrest.

One of the very few people who stood by Afinogenov in this period of utmost duress was Boris Pasternak. The two writers had known each other since 1936, when they were awarded neighboring dachas in Peredelkino. In the summer and fall of 1937 Pasternak, who at the time was working on sketches that he would later extend into the novel Doctor Zhivago, was not afraid to talk with the ostracized playwright, to take long walks with him through the village, or to visit him at his dacha. Their conversations allowed Afinogenov to share his despair and his fears with a trusted person who comforted and helped him retain his sanity. Beyond lending such vital support, Pasternak also embodied a model of personal comportment that fascinated Afinogenov. He admired Pasternak’s literary passion, which rendered him oblivious to the world: the buzz of the Moscow literary scene, the intrigues in the Writers’ Union, the feats of heroic Soviet citizens lauded by the media. Afinogenov was particularly impressed by Pasternak’s fearlessness, an attitude that was rooted in his self-mastery. He was a “living model of this vital sort of stoicism.” In the presence of people like Pasternak, “you learn the most important thing—the ability to live independently under any circumstances whatsoever.” But while he admired Pasternak’s “crystalline transparency” and exclusive dedication to his art, Afinogenov was unable and unwilling to adopt this behavioral model for himself. That Pasternak did not read newspapers or listen to the radio amazed him: “This is strange to me, who can’t live through a single day without the news.” It was imperative for Afinogenov to reside in the world, and not to situate himself outside it in a mode of stoic indifference. This world was the universe of the emerging socialist society. Even if that society barred him from recognition as a cultural leader, he could not help following its construction, as it was relayed through the lines of the newspapers and the voices of the radio.

阿菲诺格诺夫在日记中记录了他与这位诗人的会面，同时也利用日记进行其他几场对话，以应对他的命运问题。1937年9月4日，即被作家协会开除三天后，他写了一场虚构的审讯场景。这篇长记录揭示了他的思想是多么狂热地围绕着他即将到来的被捕、他将面临的指控以及他可能做出的回应。“审讯笔录”是以一个“审讯者”和第一人称叙述者（我称之为阿菲诺格诺夫）之间的对话形式写的，这清楚地表明阿菲诺格诺夫禁不住用戏剧化的方式思考自己的命运。在世界历史的舞台上，这位共产主义作家的生活正在进入决定性的篇章。他知道这是一个转折点，但其解决的形式仍不明朗。

While Afinogenov documented his encounters with the poet in his diary, he also used the diary to engage in several other conversations, to come to terms with the question of his fate. On September 4, 1937, three days after his expulsion from the Writers’ Union, he wrote an imagined interrogation scene. The long entry reveals how feverishly his thoughts revolved around his imminent arrest, the accusations he would face, and the ways he could respond to them. The “minutes of an interrogation,” written as a dialogue between an “interrogator” and a first-person narrator (whom I will call Afinogenov), also makes clear that Afinogenov could not help thinking about his personal fate in dramaturgical terms. On the world-historical stage, the life of the Communist writer was entering the decisive act. He knew it to be a turning point, but the form of its resolution remained unclear.

在这份笔录中，内务人民委员部（NKVD）的审讯者一次又一次地促使阿菲诺格诺夫承认他与“卑鄙的人民公敌”进行的“反革命工作”，并忏悔他的“巨大罪过”。阿菲诺格诺夫则声称不知道被捕的原因。他没有犯下任何反对苏联秩序的罪行，没有任何“社会罪责”。他被社会排斥是“不公正的”，尤其自1937年春天以来他已经改变了。他与之前的自我不再有任何共同之处，他暗示之前的自我并非完全清白。他与审讯者达成一致，这次审讯的关键在于阿菲诺格诺夫共产主义良知的纯洁性。像帕斯捷尔纳克一样，阿菲诺格诺夫致力于一种内在纯洁的理想，但他的纯洁不是艺术家与其作品交流的那种纯洁。阿菲诺格诺夫首先视自己为新世界的建设者。灵魂的纯洁是成为新世界一员的至关重要前提，而这只能由那个世界的守护者——内务部来认证。阿菲诺格诺夫要求审讯者对他的案件进行深入的“政治道德评估”。一旦他的纯洁得到证实，他将重新被社会及其先锋组织——共产党所接纳。阿菲诺格诺夫建议，这种测试可能需要长达三年。审讯者插话道：“或者也许五年，”他指的是阿菲诺格诺夫在有资格获得平反之前必须在监狱或流放地度过的时间。随着审讯者准备做笔记，笔录结束了：“我们现在开始吧，逐点进行。”

Time and again in this transcript, the NKVD interrogator prodded Afinogenov to admit to his “counterrevolutionary work” with “base enemies of the people” and to confess his “enormous guilt.” Afinogenov in turn professed ignorance about the reasons for his arrest. He had not committed a single crime against the Soviet order and was free of any “social guilt.” His exclusion from society was “unjust,” all the more so because he had changed since the spring of 1937. He no longer had anything in common with his previous self, who, he implied, had not been entirely guiltless. What was chiefly at stake in this interrogation, he and the interrogator agreed, was the purity of Afinogenov’s Communist conscience. Like Pasternak, Afinogenov was committed to an ideal of inner purity, but his was not the purity of the artist communing with his work. Afinogenov conceived of himself first and foremost as a builder of the new world. Purity of his soul was a vital precondition for membership in the new world, and it could only be attested by the guardians of that world—the NKVD. Afinogenov asked his interrogator for an in-depth “political-moral evaluation” of his case. Once his purity was attested he would be readmitted into society and its vanguard formation, the Communist party. This test could take as long as three years, Afinogenov suggested. “Or perhaps five,” the interrogator interjected, referring to the time Afinogenov would have to spend in prison or exile before becoming eligible for rehabilitation. The protocol ended as the interrogator readied himself to take notes: “Let us now begin, point by point.”
这场与内务部的谈话在现实中当然没有发生。阿菲诺格诺夫与审讯者达成的理解是想象出来的。考虑到由于夜复一夜等待那辆可怕的黑色轿车而产生的压力——那辆车曾好几次停在他的别墅附近带走他的邻居——阿菲诺格诺夫是否能维持其叙述者在审讯中表现出的自信，还有待观察。

This conversation with the NKVD did not, of course, take place in reality. The understanding Afinogenov reached with the interrogator was imaginary. It remained to be seen whether Afinogenov could sustain the confidence that his narrator showed under interrogation, given the pressure of waiting, night after night, for the dreaded black limousine that on several occasions had stopped near his dacha to collect one of his neighbors.
在这份笔录之后几天写下的一篇长日记揭示了审讯描述中所缺乏的绝望，但也展示了阿菲诺格诺夫相信自己如何能克服危机。虽然语气高度个人化，但该记录融合了阿菲诺格诺夫剧作的元素。它读起来就像是他所相信的未来生活戏剧将如何展开的纲要。

A long diary entry written a few days after the protocol revealed a despair that the description of the interrogation lacked, but it also showed how Afinogenov believed he could overcome his crisis. Although highly personal in tone, the entry incorporated elements of Afinogenov’s plays. It reads as an outline of the way he believed the drama of his future life would unfold.

他首先描述了自己的悲伤，并说他被一个永恒的问题所困扰：“为什么？为什么我，一个完全无辜的人和作家，现在必须像个与世隔绝的人一样生活？为什么我没有权利和所有人一起欢欣鼓舞？为什么我反而被排斥、被冷落、被怀疑……为什么？”然而，在下一句中，阿菲诺格诺夫就责备自己如此软弱和自私：“你又觉得一切都和你自己有关。你仍然无法理解这个想法：只有当正在发生的一切的目的对你变得清晰时，你才能理解一切。现在的目的是对我们苏联之家进行所有不纯洁事物的总清洗。在这次清洗期间，它将让整个国家自由、幸福地呼吸，不可避免地会有少数人无缘无故地受到伤害。”例如，这可能发生，一个杯子即便完好无损，也可能被意外扔掉。阿菲诺格诺夫推论说，如果他是一个像杯子一样的物体，他除了哀叹自己的命运之外什么也做不了：

但你终究是一个人。你必须全心全意地理解，即使你被毁灭了，也没有理由哭泣。你必须感到幸福，因为这种清洗的时候已经到来，而你被扫除不是因为某人的恶意，而是纯属巧合。难道这会成为你要求停止清除垃圾的理由吗？当然不会……当勤勉的主人在扫除垃圾时，发现窗后那只被误扔的墨水瓶，他会下令把它洗干净并放回桌子上。墨水瓶——那就是你！你还会在主人的桌子上占有一席之地很久，谁知道呢，也许他甚至会用你写出一些新的卓越思想？无论如何，目前正在发生的事情的目的是否对你清晰了？是的。你想成为这个目的的参与者，还是一个无生命的物体？当然是参与者！

这一场景在阿菲诺格诺夫的《恐惧》中很熟悉。清洗像是一场大扫除。一个特定的物体也再次出现：那是塞夫勒瓷杯，一个已褪色的贵族文化的产物，在社会主义家庭中没有位置。阿菲诺格诺夫在日记中援引它来代表一个没有生命、被动的客体，并以此相对，将自己定位为一个自觉而积极的革命主体。客体与主体的并置清楚地表明，阿菲诺格诺夫将他作为共产主义作家的角色理解为积极参与历史进程的最高形式。作为站在斯大林身边的剧作家，他被赋予了塑造社会关系并参与创造未来完美世界的造物主般的能力。

He began by describing his sadness and saying he was haunted by a perennial question: “Why? Why do I, a person and a writer who is completely innocent, now have to live like an individual cut off from the world? Why don’t I have the right to rejoice with everybody else? Why am I instead excluded, lonely, and looked upon with suspicion . . . why?” Yet in the next sentence Afinogenov scolded himself for being so weak-spirited and selfish: “You again think that everything has to do with yourself. You still can’t grasp the thought that you will understand everything only when the purpose of all that is taking place has become clear to you. That purpose now is the general purge of our Soviet house of all impurity. During this purge, which will allow the whole country to breathe freely and happily, inevitably a few will get hurt and for no reason.” It could happen, for example, that a cup would be thrown away by accident even though it was still in good condition. If he were an object like the cup, Afinogenov reasoned, he would be able to do nothing but deplore his fate:

But after all you are a human being. And you must understand with all your heart that, even if you are destroyed, there is no reason to cry. You have to be happy that the time of such a purge has come and that you have been swept away not because of somebody’s evil intentions but by pure chance. And would this be a reason for you to request a halt to the removal of garbage? Of course not . . . When the zealous master, while sweeping out the garbage, finds behind the window the inkwell that had been thrown out by mistake, he will give orders to have it washed and put back on the table. The inkwell—that is you! And you will have a place on the master’s table for a long time yet, and who knows, perhaps he will even use you to write some new remarkable thoughts? In any event, is the purpose of what’s currently going on now clear to you? Yes. Do you want to be a participant in this purpose or an in-animate object? A participant, of course!

The scenario is familiar from Afinogenov’s Fear. The purge proceeds as an act of housecleaning. A particular object resurfaces, too: it is the Sèvres cup, an artifact of a faded aristocratic culture that has no place in a socialist home. Afinogenov invoked it in his diary to represent a dead and passive object, against which he situated himself as a conscious and active revolutionary subject. The juxtaposition of object and subject makes clear that Afinogenov understood his role as a Communist writer as the highest form of active participation in the unfolding of history. As a playwright standing next to Stalin, he was endowed with a demiurgic capacity to mold social relations and partake in the creation of the perfect world of the future.

然而，这种作为共产党员和作家的自我实现的最高阶段，却包含了阿菲诺格诺夫从主体到客体的置换：变成斯大林书桌上的墨水瓶。对于凡人共产党员来说，最高层次的主体性就是变成不死苏联神灵和领袖斯大林手中的一个客体。正如阿菲诺格诺夫明确指出的，斯大林正是通过他写下了自己的思想。他是一个工具，历史——由约瑟夫·斯大林化身——通过它书写自身。因此，斯大林体制中最具创造力的作家，是其作品直接由斯大林赋予灵魂的作家。斯大林人格化了历史的革命发展，扮演着类似于黑格尔世界精神的角色，出于这个原因，阿菲诺格诺夫——以及其他苏联艺术家——的最高抱负就是占据斯大林身边的位置，以便分享他的预言眼光和变革力量。

And yet this highest stage of self-realization as a Communist and a writer entailed Afinogenov’s displacement from a subject to an object: to the inkwell on Stalin’s desk. The highest level of subjectivity for a mortal Communist was to become an object in the hands of the immortal Soviet god and leader, Stalin. As Afinogenov clearly stated, it was through him that Stalin wrote his own thoughts. He was a tool by means of which history—embodied by Joseph Stalin—wrote itself. The most creative writer in the Stalinist system was thus one whose work was directly animated by Stalin. Stalin personified history’s revolutionary development, playing a role comparable to Hegel’s world spirit, and for this reason the highest aspiration for Afinogenov—and other Soviet artists, as well—was to occupy a place near Stalin in order to share in his prophetic vision and transformative powers.
正如阿菲诺格诺夫的描述所暗示的，自我实现根据个人在苏联体制中的地位而有不同的等级。在最低层的是那些不属于党的人；由于缺乏意识，他们充其量只对历史进步有模糊的洞察，因此在很大程度上是历史的客体而非主体。党员可以对历史规律有更深刻的理解，正是这种更高的认识论地位使他们改造和完善世界的努力合法化。然而，即使是一个党员的洞察力也只是部分的，因为只有斯大林才拥有全面的洞察。

As Afinogenov’s description suggests, self-realization had different gradations according to an individual’s place in the Soviet system. In the lowest echelon were those who did not belong to the party; lacking in consciousness, they possessed at most only dim insight into historical progress and thus were largely its objects rather than its subjects. Party members could attain a much more profound understanding of the laws of history, and it was this higher epistemological status that legitimized their endeavor to transform and perfect the world. Yet even a party member’s insight was only partial, as Stalin alone possessed a total vision.
他在日记中曾将自己比作“站在脚手架上的砖瓦匠，难以理解他正在建造的东西的意义及其建筑形式”。

作为一名建筑工人，他正积极参与共产主义大厦的兴建。而且，他在脚手架上的工作场所将他提升到了很高的高度，从而赋予了他平凡的尘世生物所无法获得的视野。尽管如此，他仍然缺乏对该项目的全面概念掌握，而这只有建筑师斯大林才具备。在脚手架上工作也是危险的，因为任何粗心的举动，任何历史解释上的疏失，都可能导致致命的坠落。即便如此，砖瓦匠的这种既无限又受限且危险的天职，正是贯穿阿菲诺格诺夫整个20世纪30年代的动力。
In his diary Afinogenov once likened himself to a “bricklayer who stands on the scaffolding and has trouble understanding the meaning of what he is building and its architectural form.”

As a construction worker, he was actively taking part in the raising of the Communist edifice. What is more, his workplace on the scaffolding elevated him to great heights and thus granted him a scope of vision unavailable to ordinary earthbound beings. Still, he lacked the full conceptual grasp of the project that only the architect, Stalin, possessed. Working on the scaffolding was also perilous, as any careless move, any slip in historical interpretation, could cause a deadly fall. Even so, the bricklayer’s vocation, at once limitless, circumscribed, and dangerous, was what animated Afinogenov throughout the 1930s.

日记的这些段落提供了一个观察共产主义项目自我毁灭动态的窗口，这在大清洗期间尤为明显。这并不是说阿菲诺格诺夫被强迫服从苏联领导人颁布的历史规律。他自己积极地工作，为自己创造一种历史性的存在，将其作为自我实现的最高形式。然而，即使是阿菲诺格诺夫所奋斗的苏联秩序中的理想主体性，也无法超越对斯大林的一种客体关系，因为斯大林是历史的终极主体。这解释了为什么阿菲诺格诺夫（以及其他共产党员）接受了被党碾碎并扔进历史垃圾堆的前景：这种看似自我毁灭的行为有助于历史的最终圆满，从而满足了他作为主体为之奋斗一生的核心目的。

These passages of the diary offer a glimpse into the self-destructive dynamic of the Communist project that was particularly apparent during the Great Terror. It was not that Afinogenov was forced to submit to laws of history decreed by Soviet leaders. He himself actively worked to create a historical existence for himself as a highest form of self-realization. And yet even the ideal subjectivity in the Soviet order, for which Afinogenov strove, could not transcend an object relation toward Stalin, who was the ultimate subject of history. This explains why Afinogenov (and other Communists as well) accepted the prospect of being crushed by the party and thrown into the dustbin of history: this apparent act of self-destruction contributed to history’s eventual consummation and thereby satisfied the central purpose to which he, as subject, had devoted his life.

1937年秋天，阿菲诺格诺夫越来越确信自己很快就会被重新接纳进苏联集体。在他眼中，11月7日的革命二十周年庆典和12月初的最高苏维埃选举，代表了新社会主义社会的门槛。他预计清洗会在1937年底达到逻辑终点，届时新的政治秩序将会建立，由新一代纯洁的苏联公民充实，并摆脱过去的杂质。他相信，由于他净化自我的努力，他也能够属于这个新秩序。然而，归根结底，只有为国家进行“诚实的[文学]工作”才能确保他重新融入社会，“而不是书信、抗议、控诉。这些都没用；这种控诉和书信已经太多了。”要获得合法、有用劳动的资格，写作必须离开描述模式而变得具有变革性。他在被开除出党后撰写的请愿书和抗议书并非如此，那些文章对他案件中犯下的不公或错误喋喋不休，因此仅仅唤起了一种静态的自我感。谈论自我的唯一可接受方式是通过转型和重生的叙事。

In the fall of 1937 Afinogenov became increasingly convinced that he would soon be readmitted to the Soviet collective. In his eyes, the celebration of the twentieth anniversary of the revolution on November 7 and the elections to the Supreme Soviet in early December represented the threshold of the new socialist society. He expected the purges to reach their logical end at the close of 1937, when the new political order would have come into being, staffed by a new generation of pure Soviet citizens and freed from the impurities of the past. He, too, he believed, could belong to this new order, thanks to his efforts to purify his self. Yet, ultimately, only “honest [literary] work” for the country would ensure his reintegration into society, “not letters, protests, complaints. None of this will do; there have been too many of these complaints and letters.” To qualify as legitimate, useful labor, writing had to leave the descriptive mode and become transformative. This was not the case with the petitions and protests he had composed in the wake of his expulsion from the party, which had harped on the injustices or errors committed in his case and thus merely invoked a static sense of himself. The only acceptable way to write about the self was by means of a narrative of transformation and renewal.

阿菲诺格诺夫希望借以重新确立自己作为苏联作家地位的具体项目是一部小说——他在1935年日记中勾勒过的那部小说。1937年末，他开始认真投入这个项目。小说定名为《三年》，旨在涵盖从1934年12月到1937年底的这段时期。它将追踪主角维克多经历个人堕落、危机及随后康复的阶段。阿菲诺格诺夫试图通过这部小说传达苏联人民是如何体验斯大林主义肃反运动的。早在1935年，他的想法是探讨他对自己及周围环境感到的信仰缺失。现在，将近三年后，这个故事被目的论式地改造成了一个关于危机、解离和更高层次综合的辩证循环。同时，自传式英雄的个人故事描述了一个历史叙事。他危机与康复的三年，正好契合了更宏大的苏联危机及其解决的三年：从1934年12月因基洛夫遇刺而首次出现的反革命行动，到1937年那个胜利的秋天，届时新社会主义社会将已肃清其敌人。

The specific project through which Afinogenov hoped to redeem himself as a Soviet writer was a novel—the same novel he had sketched out in his diary in 1935. In late 1937 he began to work on the project in earnest. Entitled Three Years, the novel was to span the period from December 1934 to the end of 1937. It was to trace the development of its protagonist, Viktor, through the stages of personal degeneration, crisis, and subsequent recovery. By means of the novel, Afinogenov sought to convey how the Soviet population had experienced the Stalinist purge campaign. Back in 1935 his idea had been to address the loss of faith he felt in himself and in his environment. Now, almost three years later, the story was teleologically reworked into a dialectical cycle of crisis, dissociation, and higher synthesis. At the same time, the personal story of the autobiographical hero described a historical narrative. The three years of his crisis and recovery matched the three years of a larger Soviet crisis and its resolution: from the first appearance of counterrevolutionary action in connection with the murder of Kirov in December 1934 to the victorious autumn of 1937, when the new socialist society would have freed itself of its enemies.
阿菲诺格诺夫在日记中勾勒了这部预想作品的一个核心场景。一个人物（可能是主角）在服完流放期后回到莫斯科，遇到了一位曾与他断绝关系的旧友。“他仿佛来自另一个世界，来自坟墓之外，他急于表达一切：他已经作为一个完全不同的人回来了，现在的他和这座非凡的城市一样，发生了巨大的变化。”
计划中小说的核心主题因此是斯大林主义肃反政策所带来的自我变革劳动。

In a diary entry Afinogenov sketched out a central scene of the projected work. A character, possibly the protagonist, returns to Moscow after serving his term of exile and meets an old friend who had written him off. “It’s as if he had arrived from the world beyond the grave, and he is in a hurry to express everything: that he has returned a completely different person, that now he has changed as much as this remarkable city.”
A central theme of the planned novel was thus the self-transformative labor brought about by the Stalinist purge policies.
阿菲诺格诺夫试图刻画一个响应肃反运动号召去改造自我的个人，他通过自我锤炼，最终作为一个新人出现。显然，阿菲诺格诺夫写这部小说的目标之一是强调他自己的自我变革工作，从而支持他重返共产主义作家圈子的主张。然而，他的这种自传式练习也揭示了他试图通过写作将自己写入历史的程度。回顾过去，在他成功重生后，他被开除出党以及随后的自我锤炼，看起来就像是历史进程本身在他的身体和精神中发挥作用。

Afinogenov sought to portray an individual who, responding to the call of the purge campaign to transform himself, worked on himself and ultimately emerged as a new person. Obviously one of the goals for Afinogenov in writing the novel was to underscore his own self-transformative work and thus to support his claim for readmission into the circle of Communist writers. Yet his autobiographical exercise also revealed the extent to which he sought to write himself into history. Looked upon in retrospect, after his successful regeneration, his expulsion from the Communist party and subsequent work on himself appeared as the very course of history working through his body and spirit.

阿菲诺格诺夫的日记与他的小说创作之间有着紧密且复杂的关系。尽管日记具有高度的个人色彩，但在整个肃反期间它一直保留着鲜明的文学目的。在试图解决个人的不确定感和恐惧的同时，阿菲诺格诺夫对它们进行了构思，使之符合他小说的结构。（当然，对这两部作品的比较必然只能是推测性的，因为这部小说从未完成，只有少数章节存世，此外还有日记中记录的大纲和零散场景。）日记和小说涉及相同的个人堕落、自我锤炼和重生的主题。在这方面，日记成了阿菲诺格诺夫的自传建筑工地。它是一个自我的实验室，揭示了灵魂的内在运作，包括其阴暗面：怀疑、软弱、罪过。

Afinogenov’s diary bore a close and complex relationship to his work on the novel. Notwithstanding its highly personal character, the diary retained a distinct literary purpose throughout the entire purge period. While attempting to resolve personal uncertainties and fears, Afinogenov plotted them in such a way as to make them fit the structure of his novel. (To be sure, a comparison between the two works has to remain speculative, since the novel was never finished, and only a few chapters exist, along with outlines and scattered scenes recorded in the diary.) The diary and the novel concerned the same themes of personal degeneration, work on the self, and renewal. In this respect, the diary served Afinogenov as an autobiographical construction site. It was a laboratory of the self, revealing the inner workings of the soul, including its darker aspects: doubts, weaknesses, sins.

最重要的是，日记叙事是开放式的；它涉及一个未完成、不断扩展的自我项目。相比之下，小说虽然也处理灵魂的不纯洁，但会呈现出一幅完整、和谐的人类心理图景。它的叙事将涵盖一个完整且从一开始就预设好的堕落与重生循环，最终以英雄的救赎告终。这种区别表明阿菲诺格诺夫从未打算发表日记本身。相反，它是一个文学采石场，从中开采材料用于他的小说式自我呈现。因此，对他来说，将日记剪碎，把他认为最有价值的部分整合进他发表的作品中是有意义的。

Most important, the diary narrative was open-ended; it referred to an unfinished, ever expanding self-project. The novel, by contrast, even though it also addressed impurities of the soul, would have presented a finished, harmonious picture of the human psyche. Its narrative would have spanned a full—and, from the beginning, preordained—cycle of degeneration and regeneration, culminating in the hero’s salvation. This distinction suggests that Afinogenov never intended to publish the diary itself. Rather, it was a literary quarry from which to carve material for his novelistic self-presentation. Thus it made sense for him to cut his diary into pieces, integrating the segments he deemed most worthwhile into his published works.
在日记中为他的小说积累素材的同时，阿菲诺格诺夫告诫自己要践行绝对的真诚。只有他的写作捕捉到了他内心挣扎的本质，他恢复作家身份和作为苏联公民的自我重生的双重项目才能成功。他意识到这种对真诚的表白在肃反背景和他可能被捕的情况下所引发的问题。虚构审讯笔录的一个章节涉及了这个问题。为了证明他对自我重生的奉献精神，叙述者告诉审讯者，他记日记是为了记录他的“个人成长与发展”。

While accumulating in the diary raw material for his novel, Afinogenov admonished himself to practice utter sincerity. Only if his writings captured the essence of his inner struggle could his twofold project of restoration as a writer and self-renewal as a Soviet citizen succeed. He was aware of the questions that such professions of sincerity raised in the context of the purges and his possible arrest. A section of the invented interrogation protocol addressed this problem. To prove how dedicated he was to self-renewal, the narrator told the inter-rogator that he kept a diary in which he made notes on his “personal growth and development.”
审讯者：我不相信你的记录。
Interrogator: I don’t believe your notes.
我：我也知道这一点。
I: I knew that as well.
审讯者：为什么？
Interrogator: Why?
我：因为一旦一个人正在等待被捕并开始记笔记，我认为很明显，他是为未来的读者，也就是审讯者记的，这意味着他正在尽可能地美化一切，以证明自己的无辜。而过去的笔记，过去几年的笔记，怎么说呢，是经过“编辑”的——他进行更正、删剪、勾掉内容……你是这么想的，对吧？

I: Because once a person is waiting to be arrested and starts keeping notes, it’s clear, I should think, that he’s keeping them for the future reader, the interrogator, and that means that he’s embellishing everything as much as he can, in order to prove his innocence. And the notes from the past, from past years, how shall I put it, are “edited”—he makes corrections, makes cuts, crosses things out . . . That’s what you thought, isn’t it?
审讯者：是的。
Interrogator: Yes.

叙述者透露他也考虑过这个问题，并怀疑过是否应该停止写作。他表达的问题是，在一个高度监控和强制公开的时代，真诚意味着什么。当阿菲诺格诺夫除了文字一无所有，而这些文字的真实性将由一个疑心重重的国家读者来判定，并决定他的生死时，他如何能可信地陈述他对革命的真挚献身？对这位未来读者的意识会破坏整个真诚写作的事业。但写作的需要——为了记住他对清洗的内在体验——证明比这些怀疑更强烈。在做出这个决定时，由于意识到内务部不会相信他的陈述，他也感到宽慰。正如他的叙述者所解释的：

你不相信这些记录，嗯，这很自然，随它去吧；当然，如果你发现了有害的思想甚至轶事，那你就会相信它们，也就是说，你会以不同的方式看待它们，你会把它们视为我负罪的证明。但这也可以理解。但你不相信我为自己写的东西，我知道这一点，我考虑过这一点，这立刻让我更容易做决定——是的，我必须继续写。因为，如果我认为你会相信我的记录，那就好像我是为一个陌生人写的，那我与自己坦诚相待的能力就丧失了——无论如何，我将来都会感觉到你的眼睛盯着这些页面。但一旦我已经明白你无论如何都不会相信任何事情，而只会嘲笑你读到的我记录的内容，那么在我写日记的过程中，我就立刻从你的存在中解脱了出来，再次开始自由而简单地写作，就像我以前，在过去那些年里所做的一样。

The narrator confided that he, too, had thought about this, and had wondered whether he should stop writing. The problem he voiced was the problem of sincerity in an age of intense surveillance and mandated openness. How could Afinogenov credibly state his genuine devotion to the revolution when he had nothing but words with which to do so, and when the truth of these words, as judged by a suspicious state reader, would determine whether he lived or died? Awareness of this future reader would undermine the whole enterprise of writing sincerely. But the need to write, so as to remember his inner experience of the purge, proved stronger than these doubts. In making this decision he was also helped by the realization that the NKVD would not believe his account. As his narrator explained:

That you don’t believe these notes, well, that’s natural, so be it; of course, if you had found pernicious thoughts or even anecdotes, then you would have believed them, that is, you would view them differently, you would view them as proof of my guilt. But that’s understandable as well. But you don’t believe what I have written for myself, I knew that, I thought about that, and this immediately made it easier for me to decide the issue—yes, I must continue to write. Because, if I had thought that you would believe my notes, then it would have been as if I were writing for a stranger, and there goes my ability to be candid with myself—all the same I would have felt your eye on these pages in the future. But once I had already understood that you wouldn’t believe anything in any case and would only scoff as you read what I had recorded, then I immediately was relieved of your presence during my work on my diary and once again began to write freely and simply, as I had done before, in years past.
这并不是说阿菲诺格诺夫写日记时没有想到内务部。在他创作完审讯场景的第二天，他思考在其中起作用的更强力量是什么：“是真诚，还是想要把长期以来想和审讯者谈论的一切都倾泻到纸上的欲望。可能两者兼而有之。但那并不重要。重要的是要明白，陀思妥耶夫斯基在描述梅诗金公爵的癫痫发作时，是在写他自己和自己的感受，这不仅是一个艺术家的权利，更是他的首要义务。”

This is not to say that Afinogenov wrote his diary without the NKVD in mind. The day after he composed the interrogation scene he pondered what had been more strongly at work in it: “sincerity or the desire to pour out onto paper everything I’d wanted to talk about with the interrogator for a long time. It’s probably both things at once. But that’s not what is important. What is important is the understanding that Dostoevsky, when describing Myshkin’s epileptic fits, was writing about himself and his own feelings, and that this is not only an artist’s right, it is his primary obligation.”

阿菲诺格诺夫很难理清他体内发挥作用的政治、道德和文学压力。他究竟是为内务部还是为自己写下这份日记式的告白，这个问题无法给出一个明确的回答。被开除出党并面临被捕威胁，他在进行布尔什维克自我批评方面承受着巨大的政治压力，但与此同时，他也拥抱了这种悔罪共产党员的声音，将其视为真实的、道德的自我。更重要的是，政治和道德压力都与他作为苏联作家的任务融合在一起，即生产在社会和道德上堪称典范并具有主观真实内核的作品。阿菲诺格诺夫知道，他预想中的小说的文学价值将取决于它是否表达了他的内在真理。为了能够创作出道德典范般的文学，因此需要将自己提升到道德思考的高度。

Afinogenov had trouble disentangling the political, moral, and literary pressures at work in him. The question of whether he wrote his diaristic confession for the NKVD or for himself could not be clearly answered. Expelled from the party and under threat of arrest, he was under intense political pressure to perform Bolshevik self-criticism, but at the same time he embraced this voice of the contrite Communist as his true, moral self. What is more, both political and moral pressures fused with his task as a Soviet writer to produce literature that was socially and morally exemplary and possessed a kernel of subjective truth. Afinogenov knew that the literary worth of his projected novel would depend on whether it expressed his inner truth. To be able to write morally exemplary literature thus required raising oneself to the heights of moral thinking.

正是带着所有这些政治、道德和文学目标，阿菲诺格诺夫写下了他的日记。日记在他追求作为苏联公民、共产党员和作家的自我重生中起到了至关重要的作用。在1937年秋天，回首过去的几个月时，他写道：“记录救了我。每天晚上我都会坐下来，写下我在夜间深思熟虑并承载的所有事情，所有我痛苦和压抑的念头。一旦这些念头倾泻到纸上，我就感觉好多了。我的头脑和心脏从压力中解脱了出来；就好像另一个人承担了我阴郁念头的重担，给了我喘息之机。”日记将他从“黑色念头”的重担中解放出来，某种意义上成了垃圾堆。就像斯捷潘·波德卢布内将灵魂中积聚的所有废料都排泄到日记页上一样，阿菲诺格诺夫试图在日记中卸下他在共产主义世界中视为非法的一切，以及他视为自己不纯洁证据的一切。但与此同时，日记也为他的自我重生提供了一个视角。用他自己的话来说，一系列的记录构成了他正在跋涉的从黑暗走向光明之路上的路标。因此，阿菲诺格诺夫在整个恐怖时期记日记的主要目标之一，就是产生一份可见的自我发展记录。

It was with all of these political, moral, and literary aims in mind that Afinogenov wrote his diary. The diary played a crucial role in his quest for self-renewal as a Soviet citizen, a Communist, and a writer. In the fall of 1937, looking back at the previous months, he wrote: “The notes have saved me. Every night I would sit down and write about everything that I had given so much thought to during the night and carried in me, all my agonizing and oppressive thoughts. And as soon as these thoughts spilled onto the paper, I felt better. My mind and heart were relieved of the pressure; it was as if another person had assumed the burden of my somber thoughts and given me respite.” Freeing him from the burden of his “black thoughts,” the diary figured as a rubbish heap of sorts. Like Stepan Podlubny, who discharged onto the pages of his diary all the refuse accumulating in his soul, Afinogenov sought to unburden himself in his diary of all that was illegitimate in the Communist world and all that he regarded as evidence of his impurity. Yet at the same time the diary provided him with a perspective on his self-renewal. The sequence of entries constituted, in his own words, road marks on the path from darkness to light, along which he was traveling. One of Afinogenov’s principal goals in keeping his diary throughout the period of terror was thus the production of a visible record of self-development.

对阿菲诺格诺夫来说，布尔什维克式的自我塑造是一个永无止境的奋斗和转型过程，他是通过写作来完成的。在这条路上停下来就意味着退回到当下的、因此也是不完美的自我。而停滞无异于堕落：“现在，就在今天，例如，我带着想要以某种方式前进的愿望起床……不要停止反思，要积累我已经开始积累的东西；要不断回顾并审视自己，不允许自己变回以前的自我，哪怕一丁点儿都不行。”相反，纯洁只能在净化行动中、在与内在挥之不去的不纯洁的斗争中被体验。写作是丢弃不纯洁的一种工具，也是挖掘纯粹内在本质的一种工具，阿菲诺格诺夫将其理解为他灵魂中的共产主义本质。值得注意的是，他在1937年11月7日革命假日前夕，发现了这种纯粹的本质，即他身上“最好的部分”。这个节日旨在宣告新一代年轻领导者的诞生，也标志着阿菲诺格诺夫自己焕发青春的一天：

今天……我查阅了过去两年的笔记。仔细地，每一天。我的印象是：浪费了大量时间，无法利用环境进行工作；很多徒劳的会议，随处可见的怨恨，对更好事物的徒劳期待，我过去觉得这种“更好的事物”必然会来自别人，而我自己只要袖手旁观，等待这个人出现就行了。直到现在我才明白，最好的东西就在我体内。今年夏天，这些狂热的思考，我的笔记——它们是我身上最好的东西……前方是艰巨的工作和新的任务，它们是如此不同，比我过去做过的任何事情都要困难。未来的生活越困难，它就越丰硕。

Self-constitution in the Bolshevik vein was for Afinogenov an un-ending process of struggle and transformation, which he accomplished through writing. To stop on this road would mean to retreat into one’s present, and hence imperfect, self. And stasis was tantamount to degeneration: “Right now, today, for example, I got up with the desire to move forward somehow . . . Not to stop reflecting, and to accumulate what I’ve already begun to accumulate; to look back continually and examine myself, and not allow myself to become my former self, not even a tiny bit.” Conversely, purity could be experienced only in the act of purification, in the very struggle against lingering impurities within. Writing was a tool by which to discard impurities and also to excavate a pure inner essence, which Afinogenov understood as the Communist essence in his soul. Tellingly, he discovered this pure essence, “the best” that was in him, just before the revolutionary holiday of November 7, 1937. The holiday, which was to summon a new generation of young leaders into existence, also marked the day of Afinogenov’s own rejuvenation:

Today . . . I looked through my notes of the past two years. Carefully, every single day. My impression: an enormous amount of time wasted, an inability to make use of circumstances for work; a lot of futile meetings, of grudges at every turn, of vain expectations for something better, and it seemed to me that this “something better” would inevitably come from someone else, but that I myself should just sit there, with my arms folded, and wait for this person. Only now do I understand that the best is within me. This summer, these feverish thoughts of mine, my notes—they are the best that is in me . . . Ahead of me lie arduous work and new tasks that are so different and more difficult than anything I have done in the past. The more difficult the life ahead, the more fruitful will it be.
阿菲诺格诺夫欢迎那些标志着他已走过的距离和前方道路的障碍。他遇到的挑战、弱点和怀疑越多，他为克服它们而付出的努力就越多，他结果就会变得越纯洁。这种自我塑造和自我完善的模式，被定义为一个永无止境的工作和自我超越过程，在阿菲诺格诺夫恐怖时期的日记中体现得最为清晰，这也是他认为这段时期是他一生中最珍贵时期的主要原因。

Afinogenov welcomed the obstacles that marked the distance he had already traveled and the road still ahead of him. The more challenges, weaknesses, and doubts he encountered, the more effort he would expend to overcome them and the purer he would emerge as a result. This mode of self-constitution and self-perfection, defined as an unending process of work and self-transcendence, was most clearly present in Afinogenov’s diary of the terror period, and this was the chief reason he considered this period to be the most precious in his entire life.

Convinced that by now he had reached the level of inner purity expected of a Communist, Afinogenov petitioned for his rehabilitation in December 1937. In his diary he concluded the fateful year 1937, which had nearly destroyed him, with exclamations of gratitude for having had the opportunity to regain himself as a person and be reborn. Calling 1937 the “year of my birth,” Afinogenov undoubtedly had in mind many other party members and fellow writers for whom the year had brought destruction and death.

1938年1月18日，中央委员会发布了一项决议，承认在过去几个月里有许多共产党员被不公正地开除出党。他们是党内和国家行政机关内敌人的牺牲品，那些敌人将他们真实的面孔隐藏在热衷警惕性的表象之下。在接下来的几周里，成千上万的党员恢复了党籍，阿菲诺格诺夫也名列其中。他的日记详细描述了他的重新接纳。他被叫去参加当地区委员会的一个会议，会上党书记宣布阿菲诺格诺夫的开除及其遭遇的痛苦是仍然潜伏在苏联文学行政机关里的敌人所为。但她也断言，剧作家对他与敌人的纠葛负有个人责任：

On January 18, 1938, the Central Committee issued a resolution admitting that many Communists had been unjustly expelled from the party in the preceding months. They had been the victims of enemies within the party and the state administration who concealed their true faces behind the appearance of zealous vigilance. In the following weeks, thousands of party members were reinstated, Afinogenov among them. His diary describes his readmission in detail. He was called to a meeting in the local district committee, where the party secretary declared that Afinogenov’s expulsion and his suffering were the work of enemies still hiding in the Soviet literary administration. But she also asserted that the playwright bore a personal responsibility for his entanglements with the enemy:

“Of course, if Afinogenov had found in himself enough steadfastness to break with Averbakh and Kirshon back then [in 1932], after the Central Committee’s resolution on RAPP, he wouldn’t have gone so far in his ties to them. But I think that what he went through in these nine months is enough of a school for him. This should enable him to still write something.” Everybody agreed. My eyes became misty with tears. I muttered something, that they would not regret their decision, that I would justify their trust through all my life and work—and I was dismissed.

在日记中，阿菲诺格诺夫完全接受了对他苦难的个人责任。虽然党已经指出1937年的许多逮捕是由伪装成热诚共产党员的敌人挑起的，但他自己也太软弱、太自满了，没能注意到并干预。他写道，他的软弱实际上是他早在肃反爆发前就患上的“疾病”。起初像身体疼痛或感冒一样无害，但它反复发作，随着时间推移变得更加严重。作家组织中的敌人注意到了他的脆弱并加以利用，用他来展示他们对颠覆分子的警惕。虽然他由此将自己被开除出党定性为敌人的阴谋，但阿菲诺格诺夫并没有质疑肃反本身的审判机制。恰恰相反：他把自己的生命归功于党坚持考验其追随者的纯洁性。靠他自己，他是找不到力量从那几乎致命的腐败中解脱出来的。回首过去，他意识到自己不仅经受住了压力，而且从这九个月的炼狱中走出来时变得更好、更纯洁：“现在我……在最炽热的火中得到了证明和考验……现在我不仅是一名斯大林主义艺术家，更是一名斯大林主义钢铁般的布尔什维克！”

In the diary Afinogenov fully accepted his personal responsibility for his tribulations. While the party had indicated that many of the arrests of 1937 had been prompted by enemies masquerading as zealous Communists, he had been too weak and complacent to notice this and intervene. His weakness, he wrote, was in fact an “illness” that he had carried long before the outbreak of the purges. Harmless at first, like a body ache or a cold, it was recurrent and became more serious over time. Enemies in the Writers’ Organization noticed his vulnerability and took advantage of it, using him to demonstrate their vigilance against subversive elements. While he thus characterized his expulsion from the party as a move by his enemies, Afinogenov did not question the inquisitorial mechanism of the purge as such. On the contrary: he owed his life to the party’s insistence on testing the purity of its followers. On his own he would not have found the strength to free himself from his near-fatal corruption. Looking back he realized that not only had he withstood the pressure, he had emerged from the nine-month purgatory as a better and purer person: “Now I am . . . proven and tested in the hottest fire . . . Now I am not just a Stalinist artist but also a Bolshevik of Stalinist steel!”

阿菲诺格诺夫将他最高的感激保留给了斯大林。在对待针对阿菲诺格诺夫的控告呼吁时，斯大林没有草率行动，而是等待观察，这位苏联领袖以此表达了他对这位文学弟子的信任：“他万岁，我现在所有的思绪都指向他。愿他万岁，用他的天才统治我们，那是格鲁吉亚式的激情、俄罗斯式的理智、美国式的气魄、列宁主义的革命原则性和‘人间的人文性’的天才！”阿菲诺格诺夫暗示，苏联体制的核心是由斯大林的“人道的体恤”所定义——即他对每个愿意自我锤炼并证明自己对社会和历史有用的人的关怀。除了斯大林，阿菲诺格诺夫还觉得欠了内务人民委员部（NKVD）的人情：“也要衷心感谢卢比扬卡那边的那些人，他们正投入于铲除敌对垃圾的狂热工作中，他们没有听信那些躲在报纸笔名下的文痞们震耳欲聋的号叫；他们开展工作没有失误，不容忍错误，而是直击敌人的心脏。”剧作家也感激地记住了在他的生命中最困难时期支持过他的朋友和同事。

Afinogenov reserved his highest gratitude for Stalin. In waiting, not acting precipitously on the denunciatory appeals against Afinogenov, the Soviet leader had expressed his trust in his literary disciple: “Long live He, to whom all my thoughts are now directed. Long may he live and rule over us with his genius, the genius of Georgian passion, Russian reason, American sweep, Leninist revolutionary principledness, and Human humaneness!” At its core, Afinogenov implied, the Soviet system was defined by Stalin’s “human sensitiveness”—the fostering care he extended to each individual who was willing to work on himself and demonstrate his usefulness for society and history. Apart from Stalin, Afinogenov also felt obliged to the NKVD: “And thanks also from the bottom of my heart to those, up there at the Lubianka, engaged in their furious work rooting out the enemy riffraff, who didn’t heed the deafening howls of scribblers hiding behind their newspaper pseudonyms; who conduct their work without blunders, who don’t tolerate errors, but strike into the enemy’s very heart.” The playwright also gratefully remembered the friends and colleagues who had stood by him throughout the most difficult time of his life.

即使在平反之后，阿菲诺格诺夫仍然支持肃反运动，而运动现在的目标是那些通过告发“诚实”共产党员来谋求晋升的过激机会主义者。他渴望那些在他眼中煽动了大规模开除像他这样作家的文学官员被揭露。他对他们提出了曾用来针对他的那些指控，谴责他们对布尔什维克政府缺乏忠诚，并歪曲苏联现实。在阅读了韦尼亚明·卡维林（Veniamin Kaverin）最近的一部小说后，阿菲诺格诺夫感到“一阵愤怒，指向这些枯燥、冷漠的书籍，这些书对生活漠不关心，而[这些作者]本应为这种生活辩护，但在灵魂深处，他们并不喜欢它。”他谴责这部小说“像雅戈达的水银蒸气一样有害且有毒”，这种蒸气“慢慢吞噬灵魂，导致退化和空虚”。他的冲动是“砸碎作者的脸”，并“把所有胆敢为这部卑劣的小说浪费这么多纸张的人都拽到内务人民委员部（NKVD）去”。

Even after his rehabilitation Afinogenov supported the purge campaign, which now targeted overzealous opportunists who had furthered their careers by denouncing “honest” Communists. He longed for the unmasking of the literary officials who in his eyes had instigated the mass expulsion of writers like himself. He leveled against them the same accusations that had been made against him, condemning them for their lack of commitment to the Bolshevik government and for their distortion of Soviet reality. Reading a recent novel by Veniamin Kaverin, Afinogenov felt a “wave of fury toward these insipid, cold books, written with an indifference for life, a life that [these authors] are called upon to justify but that, in the depths of their souls, they don’t like.” He denounced the novel as “harmful and poisonous like Yagoda’s quicksilver fumes,” which “slowly engulfed the soul, causing degeneration and emptiness.” His impulse was to “smash the author’s face” and “drag to the NKVD all those who had the audacity to waste so much paper for this vile little novel.”

在恢复党籍后，阿菲诺格诺夫再次转向他的日记，打算遵循他通常的做法，剪下日记的片段并将其转移到小说大纲中。但他对大恐怖时期的记录破了例：“昨天，当我创作小说时，我对‘储备基金’——1937年的日记动了剪刀。毁掉这些页面令我悲痛。太多的东西与它们联系在一起。但我没有动那些具有决定性意义的日期和笔记。它们必须保持原样；毕竟，我记得我的新年决心是更频繁地阅读这些笔记！”在他眼中，1937年的日记作为他更新过程和他作为真正布尔什维克的新身份的物质证据而存在。在这方面，这一时期的日记并不比他的党员证逊色，在恢复党籍后的日子里，他一直以不断的惊奇注视着那本证件。阿菲诺格诺夫必须保留他生命中最关键时期的日记条目，以便知道自己确实是新苏联人之一。正是由于这个原因，他大恐怖时期的日记才得以保存至今。

In the wake of his reinstatement to the party, Afinogenov turned to his diary again, intending to follow his usual practice of cutting out segments of it and transferring them to the outline of the novel. But he made an exception for the entries from the terror period: “Yesterday, as I was working on the novel, I took scissors to the ‘reserve fund’—the diary of 1937. It grieved me to destroy the pages. So much is associated with them. But I didn’t get as far as the fateful dates and notes. They must be left intact; after all, I remember my New Year’s resolution to read these notes more often!” In his eyes, the diary of 1937 stood out as material evidence of the process of his renewal and of his new identity as a true Bolshevik. In this respect the diary of this period was no less important than his party membership booklet, which he kept looking at with unceasing wonder in the days after his reinstatement. Afinogenov had to preserve the diary entries of the most critical period in his life in order to know that he was truly one of the new Soviet men. It is only for this reason that his diary from the terror period has survived to the present day.

1938年底，阿菲诺格诺夫将新剧本《莫斯科，克里姆林宫》（Moscow, Kremlin）的草案送交给斯大林审阅。1939年新年前后，他收到了斯大林寄给“阿菲诺格诺夫同志”的一张简短便条，斯大林在信中因太忙没能阅读剧本而道歉。尽管阿菲诺格诺夫为“他的手再次给我写信”感到欣喜若狂，但斯大林的便条简明扼要地反映了这位剧作家在苏联社会的脆弱地位。斯大林承认他是同志，但没有时间阅读他的作品。阿菲诺格诺夫形式上获得了平反，但他的事业并未起色，至少没有立即起色。正如他在日记中所记，一层怀疑的阴云笼罩在他头顶；同事们会称赞他的作品，“但带有保留”；他们会承诺上演他的戏剧，但并不付诸行动；“与此同时，时间在流逝，戏却没演成。”他1939年1月的工资只有6卢布；2月只有20卢布。当同月170名苏联作家因成就获得奖励时，他并不在其中。阿菲诺格诺夫无法让另一部剧作《孩子们的母亲》（Her Children’s Mother）上演。这是他第五部未被苏联舞台接受的作品。他沉思道，在他职业生涯的早期，这样的拒绝或许是可以忍受的。但在目前的情况下，这些拒绝“有时令人筋疲力尽”。一种他的作品永远不会被允许重返舞台的感觉一直困扰着他。

In late 1938 Afinogenov sent a draft of a new play, Moscow, Kremlin, to Stalin for his evaluation. Around New Year’s of 1939 he received a brief note from Stalin, addressed to “Comrade Afinogenov,” apologizing for being too busy to read the script. Although Afinogenov was delighted that “His hand is writing to me again,” Stalin’s note indicated in a nutshell the playwright’s weak standing in Soviet society. Stalin recognized him as a comrade, but had no time to read his work. Afinogenov was formally rehabilitated, but his career did not pick up, at least not immediately. As he noted in his diary, there was a cloud of suspicion hanging above him; colleagues would praise his work, “but with a reservation”; they would promise to present his plays, but not follow through; “meanwhile, time marches on and the plays are not staged.” His salary for January 1939 consisted of 6 rubles; for February, of 20 rubles. When in the same month 170 Soviet writers received awards for achievement, he was not among them. Afinogenov was unable to get another play, Her Children’s Mother, produced. This was his fifth piece that was not accepted for the Soviet stage. Earlier in his career, he mused, such rejections might have been tolerable. But in his present situation they were “sometimes exhausting.” He was haunted by a feeling that his work would never be allowed back onto the stage.

正如以前一样，阿菲诺格诺夫将他个人关于认可与失败的沉思置于历史框架之中。他作为戏剧界弃民的境遇证实了他早先的恐惧，即他将被苏联社会发生的历史变革所席卷。他自20世纪30年代中期以来观察到的正在崛起的年轻一代，现在已经进入政治和文化生活，接替了老一代官员的位置。这些年轻人的身影让阿菲诺格诺夫敏锐地意识到自己的年龄。是的，他在清洗中重生了，但那个时期也让他付出了代价：他的恢复是“缓慢的”，他再次感到“疲倦和病态”。他，这个曾与斯大林交谈过的最年轻的剧作家，现在不得不承认新一代已经超越了他。阿菲诺格诺夫这一时期的日记充满了对自己年岁渐长、成就衰退的焦虑反思。

As before, Afinogenov situated his personal ruminations on recognition and failure in a historical frame. His situation as an outcast from the theater world confirmed his earlier fears that he would be swept away by the historical changes occurring in Soviet society. The young generation whose rise he had been observing since the mid-1930s had by now entered political and cultural life, assuming the positions of an older generation of officeholders. The specter of these young people made Afinogenov acutely aware of his own age. Yes, he had been re-born in the purge, but that period had also taken a toll: his rebound was “slow,” and he again felt “tired and sick.” He, once the youngest playwright who ever conversed with Stalin, now had to recognize that a new generation had passed him by. Afinogenov’s diary of this period is filled with anxious reflections about his advancing age and his waning achievements.

基于他认为只有青年才能赋予力量、活力以及历史乐观主义的信念，阿菲诺格诺夫采取了一个合乎逻辑但却激进的解决方案。他寻求在早逝中实现自我。他称赞自己发现了“对个人生活的漠不关心”，这援引了1937年日记中熟悉的主题；然而这一次，它并没有开启他回归苏联集体生活的进程。相反，它是为了让他为他确信即将到来的死亡做准备。他并不认为自己的死亡是自杀，即从苏联社会中自愿放逐，而是将其视为一个历史定义的生命的巅峰，以及一种永远保持年轻的方式。他1939年的日记以一系列格言结尾，最后一条写道：“英年早逝者不会老去。对我们而言，他的面容永远美好而年轻。”

Consistent with his belief that only youth imparted strength, vigor, and historical optimism, Afinogenov adopted a logical, if radical, solution. He sought to realize himself in an early death. Hailing his discovery of “indifference toward my personal life,” he invoked a theme familiar from the 1937 diary; this time, however, it did not initiate his return into the life of the Soviet collective. Rather, it was to prepare him for his death which, he was certain, would occur soon. He conceived of his death not as a suicide, a self-willed expulsion from Soviet society, but as the culminating point of a historically defined life, and as a way to remain young forever. His diary of 1939 concluded with a series of aphorisms, the last of which read: “He who dies as a young man cannot age. For us his face remains wonderful and young for all time.”

这些想法以阿菲诺格诺夫特有的方式在他的日记以及舞台作品中展开。1940年，他开始创作一部新剧《前夕》（On the Eve）——这部剧记录了他确信迫在眉睫的大战的前夕和最初几天。他在1941年2月写给作家协会国防委员会的一封信中写道，这部剧将设定在“我们目前正在接近的那些事件的前夕。它是关于人们如何根据这些事件重新审视管理个人生活及其相互关系的规范。”就像阿菲诺格诺夫在日记中一样，《前夕》的主人公学会在具有世界历史意义的时刻克服对死亡的恐惧，并理解个人生活的相对价值。在德国入侵苏联几天后，这部剧就获得了官方委托。阿菲诺格诺夫只需将他初稿中抽象的敌对势力赋予入侵的纳粹军队的面孔即可。

These thoughts developed in ways characteristic of Afinogenov, in his diary as well as in his works for the stage. In 1940 he started working on a new play, On the Eve—a play documenting the eve and the first days of the great war that, he was sure, was imminent. The play, he wrote in a note to the defense committee of the Writers’ Union in February 1941, was to be set “on the eve of those events that we are currently approaching. It is about how people in light of these events re-consider norms governing their personal lives and their mutual relations.” Just like Afinogenov in his diary, the protagonists of On the Eve learned to cope with their fear of death and to understand the relative value of a personal life in a moment of world-historical proportions. The play was officially commissioned within days after Germany’s invasion of the Soviet Union. Afinogenov had only to endow the abstract enemy forces of his first draft with the faces of the invading Nazi forces.

阿菲诺格诺夫在苏德战争爆发前就构思好了他的剧本和他个人生活的历史情节。两者在1941年6月之后都变成了现实。战争爆发十天后的1941年7月1日，他开始写新日记。他用手写在一个笔记本上，外表与前几年打字记录的散页日记截然不同。他将其命名为《最后一场战争的日记》。这个书名指的是苏联共产党人期待了至少十年的社会主义力量与帝国主义力量之间的末日决战，但它也有个人的含义：“我是在说我自己。对我来说，这是生命的最后一步。我不知道我的生命会在哪一天结束，或者我会如何死去，但我会死。我知道这一点，并且我做好了准备。”阿菲诺格诺夫写道，数百万苏联公民会活下去，但他不会是其中之一，他无法活着看到完美的未来。他并不是在战争中寻求作为“赎罪或牺牲”的死亡；相反，他将其视为“在世界历史一个命运攸关的时期所度过的生命的自然终结”。
这位剧作家迎来了自己的命运。他在1941年夏天和秋天留在莫斯科。10月中旬，他的家人被疏散到塔什干；与此同时，他被派往苏联政府部分机构迁往的古比雪夫执行任务。10月下旬，他回到被围困的首都，以获取前往英国和美国就苏联人民反抗入侵者的英勇斗争发表演讲的批准。1941年10月29日，当他在苏联共产党的机构核心——中央委员会大楼内时，被一枚德国炸弹击中身亡。

Afinogenov outlined both his play and the historical plot for his personal life before the outbreak of the German-Soviet war. Both came to life after June 1941. Ten days into the war, on July 1, 1941, he began a new diary. He wrote it by hand in a notebook, outwardly distinct from the loose sheets of paper on which he had typed his diary in preceding years. He entitled it “Diary of the Last War.” The title referred to the apocalyptic battle between the forces of socialism and imperialism that Soviet Communists had been anticipating for at least a decade, but it also had a personal meaning: “I’m speaking of myself. For me this is the last step in life. I don’t know on what day my life will end or how I will die, but I will die. I know that, and I am prepared.” Millions of Soviet citizens would live on, Afinogenov wrote, but he would not be among them, and he would not live to see the perfect future. It was not that he sought death in war “as an atonement or a sacrifice”; rather, he embraced it as a “natural end to a life lived in a fateful period of world history.”

The playwright found his fate. He remained in Moscow in the summer and fall of 1941. In mid-October his family was evacuated to Tashkent; meanwhile, he was sent on mission to Kuibyshev, where parts of the Soviet government had been relocated. In late October he returned to the beleaguered capital to obtain clearance to travel to England and the United States and give lectures on the heroic struggle of the Soviet people against the invaders. He died on October 29, 1941, struck by a German bomb, when he was in the Central Committee building, the institutional heart of the Soviet Communist party.
